Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Office Application Spawning Script Host

            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'

level: high

AutoGen Studio python process spawning non-Python child (AutoJack MCP RCE in flight) AIExploitation High
Hunts the AutoJack post-exploitation signal: the AutoGen Studio python.exe/pythonw.exe process (which hosts the MCP WebSocket handler) spawning an arbitrary child process such as calc.exe, cmd.exe, or powershell.exe. The PoC popped calc.exe under the AutoGen Studio process; any non-Python child of that process while AutoGen Studio is running an MCP route is the same shape. Rationale: Article body explicitly names the PoC: a 'Web Content Summarizer' agent caused AutoGen Studio's process to spawn calc.exe on the developer's desktop. The article also says 'launched by the AutoGen Studio process' — so the high-fidelity signal is parent=python(autogenstudio) → unusual child. PR #7362 / commit b047730 confirms the vulnerable handler shipped in 0.4.3.dev1/dev2. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/microsoft/autogen/pull/7362 • https://msrc.microsoft.com/
ATT&CKT1059 T1203
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developers running AutoGen Studio manually invoking a shell via the UI's terminal/code-exec tab
  • AutoGen Studio LLM-tool integrations that legitimately call cmd.exe/powershell.exe as a configured tool
  • Test harnesses that spawn calc.exe as a smoke-test from python wrappers
  • Jupyter-style AutoGen agents launching curl.exe to fetch sample data
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("-c \"import","jupyter","-m pytest") and FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the parent python.exe command line — confirm it loaded autogenstudio and inspect ProcessCommandLine for the child to see whether it's the PoC calc.exe popup or something weaponised (encoded PowerShell, certutil download). 2) Contain: isolate the device in Defender; kill the python.exe parent; block egress from the dev workstation pending review; capture pip freeze and confirm whether autogenstudio==0.4.3.dev1/dev2 is installed. 3) Hunt: search 30d for the same parent→child shape across other dev workstations; check DeviceNetworkEvents for the python.exe parent connecting to attacker URLs immediately before the spawn; verify no installs of vulnerable pre-release versions remain.

| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python.exe","pythonw.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("autogenstudio","autogen_studio","autogenstudio.web","autogenstudio.cli")
| where FileName !in~ ("python.exe","pythonw.exe","conhost.exe","pip.exe","py.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("calc.exe","cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","certutil.exe","bitsadmin.exe","curl.exe","notepad.exe","calculator.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessTokenElevation !~ "TokenElevationTypeFull"

          ParentImage = InitiatingProcessFolderPath,

          ChildCmd = ProcessCommandLine,

| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine

title: AutoGen Studio Python Spawning Unusual Child (AutoJack RCE)
id: 7f3e0c1a-2c4f-4b18-9a30-2d8c5e4b6a01
description: Detects the AutoJack post-exploitation pattern where AutoGen Studio (Python-hosted MCP WebSocket route) spawns a non-Python child such as calc.exe, cmd.exe or powershell.exe — matching the published PoC that popped calc.exe under the AutoGen Studio process.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/autojack-attack-lets-one-web-page.html
  - https://github.com/microsoft/autogen/pull/7362
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/19
tags:
  - attack.t1059
  - attack.t1203
  - attack.execution
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_parent:
    ParentImage|endswith:
      - '\python.exe'
      - '\pythonw.exe'
    ParentCommandLine|contains:
      - 'autogenstudio'
      - 'autogen_studio'
  selection_child:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\calc.exe'
      - '\cmd.exe'
      - '\powershell.exe'
      - '\pwsh.exe'
      - '\mshta.exe'
      - '\rundll32.exe'
      - '\regsvr32.exe'
      - '\wscript.exe'
      - '\cscript.exe'
      - '\certutil.exe'
      - '\bitsadmin.exe'
      - '\curl.exe'
  condition: selection_parent and selection_child
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @ParentImage:(*\python.exe OR *\Python.exe OR *\pythonw.exe) @ParentCommandLine:(*autogenstudio* OR *autogen_studio*) @Image:(*\calc.exe OR *\CALC.EXE OR *\cmd.exe OR *\powershell.exe OR *\PowerShell.exe OR *\pwsh.exe OR *\mshta.exe OR *\rundll32.exe OR *\regsvr32.exe OR *\wscript.exe OR *\cscript.exe OR *\certutil.exe OR *\bitsadmin.exe OR *\curl.exe)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| ParentBaseFileName=/pythonw?\.exe$/i
| regex("autogenstudio|autogen_studio", field=ParentCommandLine)
| ImageFileName=/\\(calc|cmd|powershell|pwsh|mshta|rundll32|regsvr32|wscript|cscript|certutil|bitsadmin|curl)\.exe$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ParentBaseFileName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())

Browser process connecting to localhost MCP WebSocket on AutoGen Studio port AIDelivery Medium
Hunts the AutoJack delivery primitive: a browsing agent (or browser process) opening a WebSocket to a local AutoGen Studio MCP endpoint on 127.0.0.1. The vulnerable handler lives behind ws://127.0.0.1:<port>/mcp/* and trusts localhost without auth — a browser-initiated connection from JavaScript on an attacker page is the exact trigger. Rationale: Article describes the chain: 'JavaScript can reach a privileged local service on the same machine' over the MCP WebSocket and the localhost check is bypassed because the browser agent and AutoGen Studio share the same host. Browser → 127.0.0.1:<autogen-port> is the network-layer signal that precedes the RCE. AutoGen Studio defaults to port 8081. Cross-checked against: • https://microsoft.github.io/autogen/ • https://github.com/microsoft/autogen/pull/7362
ATT&CKT1190 T1559
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developers manually opening http://127.0.0.1:8081 in the browser to use the AutoGen Studio UI
  • Local browser-based dev tools (Streamlit, FastAPI Swagger UI) on the same ports
  • Jupyter notebooks proxied through the browser hitting localhost
  • Browser DevTools live-reload polling local ports
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "--app=http://127.0.0.1"
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the URL the browser had open at the time (DeviceProcessEvents for the browser parent's cmdline / Url) — if it's an external attacker page rather than http://127.0.0.1:8081/, escalate immediately. 2) Contain: isolate the device, kill the AutoGen Studio python process, capture the WebSocket frames if pcap is available. 3) Hunt: correlate with the AutoJack execution UC for child process spawn within 60s of the localhost connection; check for downloads from the page in DeviceFileEvents; sweep the org for installed vulnerable autogenstudio==0.4.3.dev* via Defender TVM.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where RemoteIP in ("127.0.0.1","::1","0.0.0.0")
| where RemotePort in (8081,8000,8001,8080,8088)
| join kind=inner (
    DeviceProcessEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python.exe","pythonw.exe")
    | where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("autogenstudio","autogen_studio")
    | project DeviceId, AutoGenSeen = Timestamp
  ) on DeviceId
| where Timestamp between (AutoGenSeen - 1h .. AutoGenSeen + 1h)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          RemoteIP, RemotePort, LocalPort
| order by Timestamp desc
let AutoGenHosts = WindowsEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where EventData has_any ("autogenstudio","autogen_studio")
| project Computer, _t = TimeGenerated;
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where SourceProcessName has_any ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe")
| where DestinationIP in ("127.0.0.1","::1")
| where DestinationPort in (8081,8000,8001,8080,8088)
| join kind=inner AutoGenHosts on $left.SourceHostName == $right.Computer
| project TimeGenerated, SourceHostName, SourceProcessName, DestinationIP, DestinationPort
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:3 @Image:(*\chrome.exe OR *\Chrome.exe OR *\msedge.exe OR *\firefox.exe OR *\brave.exe) @DestinationIp:(127.0.0.1 OR ::1) @DestinationPort:(8081 OR 8000 OR 8001 OR 8080 OR 8088)
#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4
| ContextImageFileName=/\\(chrome|msedge|firefox|brave|arc)\.exe$/i
| RemoteAddressIP4="127.0.0.1"
| RemotePort=/^(8081|8000|8001|8080|8088)$/
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, RemotePort], function=count())

Installation of vulnerable AutoGen Studio pre-release (0.4.3.dev1 / 0.4.3.dev2) AIWeaponization High
Detects pip installing the two known-vulnerable pre-release builds of autogenstudio that shipped the unauthenticated MCP WebSocket handler. Neither build has been yanked from PyPI and there is no patched release yet — install of either is a direct exposure to the AutoJack chain. Rationale: Article calls out the exact two PyPI builds carrying the vulnerable handler — 0.4.3.dev1 and 0.4.3.dev2 — and notes pip will only fetch them with --pre or an explicit pin. The Hacker News confirmed inspection of both builds. These are concrete supply-chain IOCs, not general behaviour. Cross-checked against: • https://pypi.org/project/autogenstudio/#history • https://github.com/microsoft/autogen/pull/7362
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1059.006
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researchers intentionally installing the vulnerable build in a sandbox to validate the report
  • Reverse-engineering / DFIR labs reproducing the PoC
  • Internal red team setting up an AutoJack lab
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the device + user; run `pip show autogenstudio` to confirm the installed version; check whether the device is also running a browsing agent (Playwright/Selenium/AutoGen browser tool). 2) Contain: uninstall autogenstudio==0.4.3.dev*; if AutoGen Studio is needed, replace with `pip install git+https://github.com/microsoft/autogen.git@b047730#subdirectory=python/packages/autogen-studio` per the article; isolate the device until verified. 3) Hunt: pivot to the execution UC for any AutoJack post-exploit child spawn on the same host in the install window; sweep the org with Defender TVM software inventory query for autogenstudio version pattern 0.4.3.dev*.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("pip.exe","pip3.exe","python.exe","pythonw.exe","py.exe","uv.exe","poetry.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "autogenstudio"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("0.4.3.dev1","0.4.3.dev2","--pre","0.4.3.dev")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("install","add","sync")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\pip.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\pip3.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\python.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\pythonw.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\uv.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\poetry.exe"
| where CommandLine has "autogenstudio"
| where CommandLine has_any ("0.4.3.dev1","0.4.3.dev2","--pre","0.4.3.dev")
| where CommandLine has_any ("install","add","sync")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

SocGholish fake-update JS dropped to Downloads by a web browser AIDelivery Medium
Hunts the initial SocGholish file-write where a victim's browser delivers a JavaScript file with browser-update-themed naming (Update.js, Chrome.Update.js, Firefox.js, Opera.Update.js) into the user's Downloads folder from a compromised WordPress site. Article confirms the lure theme is fake updates for Chrome/Firefox; Reliaquest/Proofpoint corroborate the exact filename pattern. Rationale: Article names Chrome/Firefox fake-update lures delivered via compromised WordPress. Reliaquest and Proofpoint document the exact filename patterns (Update.js, Opera.Update.js, Firefox.js). Hunting tier because dev-tools and JS library downloads create FP volume that needs analyst review. Cross-checked against: • https://reliaquest.com/blog/socgholish-fakeupdates/ • https://www.proofpoint.com/us/blog/threat-insight/part-1-socgholish-very-real-threat-very-fake-update • https://redcanary.com/threat-detection-report/threats/socgholish/ • https://www.infoblox.com/blog/threat-intelligence/hot-take-operation-endgame-vs-socgholish/
ATT&CKT1189 T1204.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Web developer downloading js libraries from npm/GitHub mirrors with 'update' in name
  • Browser dev-tools 'Save As' of a page's update script
  • Vendor portals that distribute JS-based auto-updaters via web download (rare)
  • User saving a publicly-served updater from a SaaS UI that names files with 'update' (e.g. some SaaS bookmarklets)
  • QA testers downloading test JS bundles from internal sites
Suppression filter
| where FileOriginUrl !has "chrome.google.com" and FileOriginUrl !has "mozilla.org" and FileOriginUrl !has "opera.com" and FileOriginUrl !has "github.com"
Response runbook
1. TRIAGE: Pivot on the FileOriginUrl/referrer — was the source a legitimate vendor (chrome.google.com / mozilla.org) or a random third-party WordPress site? Hash the JS and submit to VT/ANY.RUN; SocGholish JS shows heavy obfuscation and PowerShell strings. 2. CONTAIN: If the JS was executed (check DeviceProcessEvents for wscript.exe FileName==<dropped>.js on same DeviceId within 30 min), isolate the host via Defender Live Response; revoke browser session tokens and force user re-auth. 3. HUNT: Block the source WordPress domain at proxy, search the org for any other host that downloaded from the same FileOriginUrl, and pivot on SocGholish UC2-UC5 (wscript→PowerShell→client32.exe). Report compromised WordPress URL to Shadowserver/Silent Push.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType == "FileCreated"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe","arc.exe")
| where FolderPath has @"\Downloads\"
| where FileName endswith ".js"
| where FileName has_any ("update","chrome","firefox","opera","browser")
| where FileName !endswith ".js.map"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, FolderPath, FileOriginUrl, FileOriginReferrerUrl, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventType == "FileCreated"
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| where TargetFilePath has @"\Downloads\"
| where TargetFileName endswith ".js"
| where TargetFileName has_any ("update","chrome","firefox","opera","browser")
| where TargetFileName !endswith ".js.map"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256
title: SocGholish Fake Browser Update JavaScript Dropped by Browser
id: 5e3a8e4c-7d2b-4c2a-8e5f-fa3b8c5e9d10
description: Detects a web browser writing a browser-update-themed JavaScript file to a user's Downloads folder, the canonical SocGholish (FakeUpdates) initial-access drop from compromised WordPress sites disrupted by Operation Endgame.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/operation-endgame-disrupts-socgholish.html
  - https://reliaquest.com/blog/socgholish-fakeupdates/

tags:

  - attack.t1204.002

logsource:
  category: file_event
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_browser:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\chrome.exe'
      - '\msedge.exe'
      - '\firefox.exe'
      - '\brave.exe'

    TargetFilename|endswith: '.js'
  selection_lure:
    TargetFilename|contains:
      - 'update'
      - 'chrome'
      - 'firefox'
      - 'opera'
      - 'browser'
  filter_sourcemap:
    TargetFilename|endswith: '.js.map'
  condition: all of selection_* and not filter_sourcemap
falsepositives:
  - Web developers downloading JS libraries from code-hosting sites
  - Browser dev-tools saving page source
level: medium
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 @Image:(*\chrome.exe OR *\Chrome.exe OR *\msedge.exe OR *\MsEdge.exe OR *\firefox.exe OR *\Firefox.exe OR *\brave.exe OR *\opera.exe) @TargetFilename:(*\Downloads\*update*.js OR *\Downloads\*Update*.js OR *\Downloads\*chrome*.js OR *\Downloads\*Chrome*.js OR *\Downloads\*firefox*.js OR *\Downloads\*Firefox*.js OR *\Downloads\*opera*.js OR *\Downloads\*Opera*.js) -@TargetFilename:*.js.map
#event_simpleName=FileWritten
| ContextImageFileName=/\\(chrome|msedge|firefox|brave|opera)\.exe$/i
| TargetFileName=/\\Downloads\\.*(update|chrome|firefox|opera|browser).*\.js$/i
| NOT TargetFileName=/\.js\.map$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, TargetFileName], function=count())

| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.action=created Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe") Filesystem.file_path="*\\Downloads\\*" Filesystem.file_name="*.js" (Filesystem.file_name="*update*" OR Filesystem.file_name="*chrome*" OR Filesystem.file_name="*firefox*" OR Filesystem.file_name="*opera*" OR Filesystem.file_name="*browser*") by host Filesystem.user Filesystem.process_name Filesystem.file_name Filesystem.file_path | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
SocGholish JS stager: wscript.exe executing .js from Downloads with browser/explorer parent AIExploitation High
Detects the SocGholish post-click execution where the user double-clicks the downloaded fake-update JavaScript and Explorer/browser launches wscript.exe against a .js file in Downloads. This is the highest-fidelity SocGholish endpoint signature documented by Proofpoint, Reliaquest, and Red Canary. Rationale: Article confirms the JavaScript-downloader theme. Reliaquest's 2026 SocGholish chain analysis names the exact triggers: 'end-users executing JavaScript scripts with filenames that relate to known browsers' via wscript. Parent=explorer/browser + child=wscript + .js in Downloads is documented as the canonical SocGholish signature with very low FP rate. Cross-checked against: • https://reliaquest.com/blog/socgholish-fakeupdates/ • https://redcanary.com/threat-detection-report/threats/socgholish/ • https://www.proofpoint.com/us/blog/threat-insight/part-1-socgholish-very-real-threat-very-fake-update
ATT&CKT1059.007 T1204.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer running test JS via Windows Script Host from a Downloads folder
  • Legitimate vendor installer that drops a .js into Temp and shells out to wscript (vanishingly rare)
  • Browser-based 'open with' helpers when a user explicitly chooses wscript
  • IT helpdesk diagnostic .js scripts run from a Downloads share
Response runbook
1. TRIAGE: Read the .js content via Defender Live Response — SocGholish JS is heavily obfuscated, contains PowerShell strings, and references SVG/IWR. Pivot on the same DeviceId for DeviceProcessEvents within +5 min looking for a powershell.exe child of this wscript (see UC3). 2. CONTAIN: Isolate the device, kill the wscript.exe process tree, quarantine the .js, force user password reset (SocGholish frequently chains to credential theft/LockBit). 3. HUNT: Search across the tenant for any other wscript.exe with a Downloads-resident .js in the last 14d; pivot on InitiatingProcessRemoteSession to spot RDP-assisted runs; check if the same FileOriginUrl seeded other hosts (UC1 join).
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName =~ "wscript.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("explorer.exe","chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has ".js"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any (@"\Downloads\", @"\AppData\Local\Temp\")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          Parent = InitiatingProcessFileName,
          ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          Child = FileName,
          ChildCmd = ProcessCommandLine,
          SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\wscript.exe"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\\explorer.exe","\\chrome.exe","\\msedge.exe","\\firefox.exe","\\brave.exe","\\opera.exe")
| where CommandLine has ".js"
| where CommandLine has_any ("\\Downloads\\","\\AppData\\Local\\Temp\\")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
title: SocGholish Wscript Executing JS from Downloads (Browser or Explorer Parent)
id: 8b4e2c91-3f6a-4d8b-9c1e-2a7b5d3f8e02
description: Detects wscript.exe spawned by Windows Explorer or a web browser, executing a JavaScript file in the user's Downloads or Temp directory. This is the SocGholish (FakeUpdates) post-click stager signature.

level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @Image:(*\wscript.exe OR *\WScript.exe OR *\WSCRIPT.EXE) @ParentImage:(*\explorer.exe OR *\Explorer.EXE OR *\chrome.exe OR *\Chrome.exe OR *\msedge.exe OR *\firefox.exe OR *\Firefox.exe OR *\brave.exe OR *\opera.exe) @CommandLine:(*\\Downloads\\*.js* OR *\\AppData\\Local\\Temp\\*.js*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| ImageFileName=/\\wscript\.exe$/i
| ParentBaseFileName=/^(explorer|chrome|msedge|firefox|brave|opera)\.exe$/i
| regex("\\\\(Downloads|Temp)\\\\.*\\.js", field=CommandLine, flags="i")

SocGholish PowerShell second stage: wscript spawning PowerShell with Invoke-WebRequest to .svg payload AIInstallation High
Detects the SocGholish JS stager's second stage where the wscript-executed .js calls PowerShell's Invoke-WebRequest to download a file with a Scalable Vector Graphics (SVG) extension and pipes it to Invoke-Expression. The .svg-extension PowerShell payload is a distinctive SocGholish trade-craft documented by Reliaquest's 2026 chain analysis. Rationale: Article describes JS downloader fetching next-stage payloads. Reliaquest's 2026 analysis specifically calls out 'Update.js leverages PowerShell's Invoke-WebRequest to download a PowerShell script with a Scalable Vector Graphics (SVG) extension'. The wscript→powershell→IWR→.svg→IEX chain is a vanishingly rare signature outside SocGholish. Cross-checked against: • https://reliaquest.com/blog/socgholish-fakeupdates/ • https://www.globalsecuritymag.com/new-socgholish-infection-chain-discovered-reliaquest.html • https://alertoverload.com/posts/2025/04/socgholish/
ATT&CKT1059.001 T1105 T1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer scripting that legitimately downloads SVG icons via PowerShell IWR (unlikely with wscript parent)
  • Custom internal IT tool that wraps PowerShell in a JS wrapper for asset fetching
  • Vendor installer using JS+PowerShell for icon updates (no observed legitimate vendor uses this chain)
Suppression filter
| where ProcessCommandLine !has "github.com" and ProcessCommandLine !has "cdn.jsdelivr.net" and ProcessCommandLine !has "raw.githubusercontent.com"
Response runbook
1. TRIAGE: Extract the SVG URL from ProcessCommandLine; capture the file via curl/Defender Live Response and analyse — SocGholish wraps its PowerShell payload in SVG XML wrappers. Pivot on DeviceNetworkEvents same DeviceId same minute for the IWR egress to identify the C2 host. 2. CONTAIN: Isolate device, kill the powershell.exe and parent wscript.exe, block the SVG-host domain at proxy/DNS, force credential reset. 3. HUNT: Across the tenant, search for any powershell.exe with `.svg` in the cmdline regardless of parent (some variants spawn from explorer); search for the SVG-host domain in DeviceNetworkEvents; pivot to UC4/UC5 to find NetSupport drops on the same host.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("Invoke-WebRequest","iwr ","IEX","Invoke-Expression")
| where ProcessCommandLine has ".svg"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          ChildCmd = ProcessCommandLine,
          Grandparent = InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith_cs "\\powershell.exe" or NewProcessName endswith_cs "\\pwsh.exe"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\\wscript.exe","\\cscript.exe")
| where CommandLine has_any ("Invoke-WebRequest","iwr ","IEX","Invoke-Expression")
| where CommandLine has ".svg"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
title: SocGholish PowerShell Stager Fetching SVG-Extension Payload
id: 1d7c4f82-9b1e-4a3d-bf52-6a8c9e2d4f17
description: Detects PowerShell spawned by Windows Script Host (wscript or cscript) calling Invoke-WebRequest against a URL whose path ends with .svg, then piping into Invoke-Expression. This is the SocGholish (FakeUpdates) second-stage downloader signature.
references:

source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @Image:(*\powershell.exe OR *\PowerShell.exe OR *\POWERSHELL.EXE OR *\pwsh.exe) @ParentImage:(*\wscript.exe OR *\WScript.exe OR *\WSCRIPT.EXE OR *\cscript.exe OR *\CScript.exe) @CommandLine:(*Invoke-WebRequest* OR *"iwr "* OR *Invoke-Expression* OR *IEX*) @CommandLine:(*.svg*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| ImageFileName=/\\(powershell|pwsh)\.exe$/i
| ParentBaseFileName=/^(wscript|cscript)\.exe$/i
| regex("(Invoke-WebRequest|iwr |Invoke-Expression|IEX)", field=CommandLine, flags="i")

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=t count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe") Processes.parent_process_name IN ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe") (Processes.process="*Invoke-WebRequest*" OR Processes.process="*IWR *" OR Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*") Processes.process="*.svg*" by host Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)

NetSupport RAT client32.exe executing from AppData Roaming subfolder (SocGholish follow-on) AICommand & Control High
Detects execution of the NetSupport Manager client binary (client32.exe) from a non-standard location under %AppData%\Roaming, where SocGholish drops the renamed/legitimate NetSupport RAT after the JS+PowerShell chain completes. Legitimate NetSupport installs under Program Files; AppData\Roaming\<random>\client32.exe is the SocGholish-delivered shape. Rationale: Article calls out NetSupport RAT as a follow-on payload. OpenText, Cyble, and Picus all document SocGholish dropping client32.exe to %AppData%\Roaming\<random>\ rather than the legitimate Program Files install path. Same-name-wrong-path is a high-fidelity T1036.005 signal. Cross-checked against: • https://blogs.opentext.com/netsupport-remote-access-trojan-rat-delivered-through-fake-browser-updates-by-socgholish-threat-actors/ • https://cyble.com/blog/netsupport-rat-distributed-via-socgholish/ • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/detecting-evolving-threats-netsupport-rat/ • https://www.picussecurity.com/resource/blog/how-netsupport-rat-abuses-legitimate-remote-admin-tool
ATT&CKT1219 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • IT team portable-deploying NetSupport Manager to AppData for testing
  • NetSupport Manager 'roaming profile' install scenario (uncommon — usually MSI to Program Files)
  • Pen-test/red-team using NetSupport for authorised C2 simulation
  • Education vertical using NetSupport School in non-standard install dir
Suppression filter
| where ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName !has "NetSupport" or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","cmd.exe","explorer.exe")
Response runbook
1. TRIAGE: Check the SHA256 against the org's authorised-software allowlist and against VT — legitimate NetSupport binaries are signed by 'NetSupport Ltd'; SocGholish drops may carry a valid sig but in the wrong path. Inspect the sibling files (client32.ini, NSM.LIC) — the .ini carries the C2 gateway address. 2. CONTAIN: Isolate host via Defender, kill client32.exe + child shells, capture the directory contents (client32.exe + client32.ini + pcicapi.dll + HTCTL32.DLL) for analysis, force user credential reset. 3. HUNT: Across the tenant, look for any client32.exe execution outside Program Files in the last 90d; pivot on the gateway address parsed from client32.ini to other infected hosts; correlate back through UC2/UC3 on the same device to confirm SocGholish chain (vs other RAT vector).
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "client32.exe"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\AppData\Roaming\", @"\AppData\Local\", @"\ProgramData\", @"\Users\Public\")
| where FolderPath !has @"\Program Files"
| where InitiatingProcessVersionInfoCompanyName !has "NetSupport"
   or isempty(ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          Parent = InitiatingProcessFileName,
          ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          Path = FolderPath,
          ChildCmd = ProcessCommandLine,
          ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName,
          SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\client32.exe"
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\\AppData\\Roaming\\","\\AppData\\Local\\","\\ProgramData\\","\\Users\\Public\\")
| where NewProcessName !has "\\Program Files"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
title: NetSupport RAT client32 Executed from AppData (SocGholish Follow-on)

NetSupport RAT Run-key persistence pointing to client32.exe in AppData AIInstallation High
Detects the SocGholish-delivered NetSupport RAT persistence pattern: a value written to HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run whose data references client32.exe inside AppData\Roaming. Per OpenText/Cyble, the value name is a short random string (e.g. rMBhIvmVX) pointing to %AppData%\Roaming\<random-folder>\client32.exe. Rationale: Article identifies NetSupport RAT as a SocGholish payload. OpenText/Cyble publish the exact persistence indicator: HKCU\...\Run\<random> = C:\Users\<user>\AppData\Roaming\<random>\client32.exe. A Run-key value with this exact string shape is essentially a one-to-one NetSupport-RAT-via-SocGholish indicator. Cross-checked against: • https://blogs.opentext.com/netsupport-remote-access-trojan-rat-delivered-through-fake-browser-updates-by-socgholish-threat-actors/ • https://cyble.com/blog/netsupport-rat-distributed-via-socgholish/ • https://www.picussecurity.com/resource/blog/how-netsupport-rat-abuses-legitimate-remote-admin-tool
ATT&CKT1547.001 T1219
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorised portable NetSupport Manager install via Run-key on a roaming-profile workstation
  • IT-managed NetSupport School deployment that uses AppData install for non-admin users
  • Red-team operator authorised use of NetSupport for engagement
  • Migration of a legitimate NetSupport install from Program Files to AppData by a sysadmin
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("msiexec.exe","NSM.exe","setup.exe") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("powershell","wscript","cscript")
Response runbook
1. TRIAGE: Inspect the InitiatingProcessFileName that wrote the Run value — legitimate NetSupport installers are NSM.msi or NetSupportSchool.msi; SocGholish writes are typically from powershell.exe, wscript.exe, or reg.exe. Cross-check the referenced client32.exe against UC4. 2. CONTAIN: Delete the Run-key value via Defender Live Response, isolate device, kill client32.exe processes, force user reset. Capture client32.ini for the C2 gateway address and block it at the perimeter. 3. HUNT: Across the tenant, search for any HKCU Run value whose data contains client32.exe in the last 90d; pivot on the writing process (the same wscript/powershell from UC2-3 chain); search DeviceFileEvents for client32.ini writes in AppData to find dormant infections that haven't yet executed.
DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("RegistryValueSet","RegistryValueCreated")
| where RegistryKey has @"\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run"
| where RegistryValueData has "client32.exe"
| where RegistryValueData has_any (@"\AppData\Roaming\", @"\AppData\Local\", @"\ProgramData\")
| where RegistryValueData !has @"\Program Files"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          RegistryKey, RegistryValueName, RegistryValueData
| order by Timestamp desc
ImRegistryEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventType in ("RegistryValueSet","RegistryValueCreated")
| where RegistryKey has @"\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run"
| where RegistryValueData has "client32.exe"
| where RegistryValueData has_any (@"\AppData\Roaming\", @"\AppData\Local\", @"\ProgramData\")
| where RegistryValueData !has @"\Program Files"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, RegistryKey, RegistryValue, RegistryValueData

id: 4a2b8c91-5e7d-43f1-9a82-d6c4f3e8b21a

LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High

Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"

SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

CISA Warns Fortinet Customers as FortiBleed Hits 86,644 FortiGate Devices

The Hacker News
2026-06-19 7 use cases 3 techniques 7 kill-chain phases detected

The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) on Thursday urged Fortinet customers with FortiGate appliances to take steps to secure against ongoing malicious activity aimed at thousands of internet-accessible devices. The sweeping campaign, believed to be the work of Russian-speaking threat actors, has been codenamed FortiBleed. The number of compromised devices stands at

ATT&CKT1190 T1555.003 T1566
Click any ATT&CK pill below to open it on the Matrix

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] FortiGate VPN/admin credential-stuffing burst from single source IP · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] FortiGate successful login using default/built-in admin account from external IP · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] FortiGate config change within 10 minutes of admin login from a new external IP · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs
FortiGate VPN/admin credential-stuffing burst from single source IP AIDelivery High
Detects a spray of failed FortiGate SSL VPN or admin-portal authentications from a single external source within a short window — the FortiBleed first-stage credential-stuffing pattern against internet-facing FortiGate devices. Hunts the bespoke spray tool that walks leaked Fortinet password lists. Rationale: Article specifies a 'bespoke tool to spray those identified endpoints with known login and password combinations' against Fortinet remote login endpoints. SOCRadar reports 86,644 compromised devices following this pattern. Cross-checked NCSC advisory describing brute-force/dictionary/credential-stuffing on Fortinet VPN gateways and Arctic Wolf write-up of the campaign. Cross-checked against: • https://www.ncsc.gov.uk/news/global-credential-stuffing-campaign-fortinet • https://arcticwolf.com/resources/blog/cve-2025-25257-fortinet-fortiweb-pre-auth-rce-vulnerability/ • https://socradar.io/
ATT&CKT1110.003 T1110.004 T1133
Data sourcesAuthentication Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Mass password reset day where every employee fat-fingers SSL VPN login from corporate egress NAT
  • Automated vulnerability scanner (Qualys/Nessus/Rapid7) authenticated-scan probe against the management interface
  • Misconfigured client application repeatedly retrying with cached bad credentials
  • Third-party penetration test from a known consultant source IP
  • CGNAT / mobile-carrier shared NAT where many real users hit the firewall from one IP
Suppression filter
| where SourceUserName !in~ ("", "-") and SourceIP !in (dynamic(["<scanner_ip_1>","<pentest_ip>"])) and FortiGates !has_any ("lab-","test-")
Response runbook
1. Triage: Pull all CommonSecurityLog hits for the offending SourceIP across last 24h; identify whether any FailedAttempt was followed by a successful login (Activity has 'login' and EventOutcome 'success') and which usernames succeeded. 2. Contain: Block SourceIP at the edge / GeoIP-block the source country if external; force-rotate passwords for any user that succeeded and terminate active SSL VPN sessions on the targeted FortiGate via 'execute vpn ssl-vpn list' then 'execute vpn ssl-vpn del-tunnel'. 3. Hunt: Pivot on succeeded usernames into AAD/AD logon events for the same accounts, check FortiGate config-change audit log for the device for unauthorized admin changes, and grep historical SSL VPN logs for the same usernames hitting the appliance from previously unseen geolocations.
let WindowMin = 5m;
let FailThreshold = 20;
let UserThreshold = 10;
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where DeviceVendor =~ "Fortinet" and DeviceProduct in~ ("Fortigate","FortiGate")
| where Activity has_any ("login failed","ssl vpn login fail","admin login failed","authentication failure","login","ssl-login-fail") or DeviceEventClassID in ("32002","32003","0102043008","0100032003","0101039425")
| where EventOutcome in~ ("failure","failed","deny","denied") or DeviceAction in~ ("login_failed","ssl_login_fail","deny")
| where ipv4_is_private(SourceIP) == false
| summarize FailedAttempts = count(),
            UsersTried = dcount(SourceUserName),
            UserList = make_set(SourceUserName, 50),
            FortiGates = make_set(DeviceExternalID, 10),
            FortiGateHosts = make_set(DestinationHostName, 10),
            FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated),
            LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated)
            by SourceIP, bin(TimeGenerated, WindowMin)
| where FailedAttempts >= FailThreshold or UsersTried >= UserThreshold
| order by FailedAttempts desc

FortiGate successful login using default/built-in admin account from external IP AIExploitation Medium
Detects a successful FortiGate authentication using the well-known 'admin' or other Fortinet built-in system accounts originating from a public IP. SOCRadar's FortiBleed dataset shows 35% of compromised credentials are generic admin accounts and 28.3% are built-in Fortinet system accounts, so any external successful login to one is high-priority. Rationale: Article + SOCRadar quote both name 'generic admin accounts' and 'built-in Fortinet system accounts' as 63.3% of compromised credentials, citing a 'widespread failure to rename default accounts'. Account list (admin/maintainer/fortinet/diag/super_admin/prof_admin) is the documented Fortinet built-in set per Fortinet PSIRT default-account guidance. Hudson Rock and NCSC writeups corroborate. Cross-checked against: • https://www.ncsc.gov.uk/news/global-credential-stuffing-campaign-fortinet • https://www.fortiguard.com/psirt • https://hudsonrock.com/blog/
ATT&CKT1078.001 T1133 T1078.004
Data sourcesAuthentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate admin still using default 'admin' username from a home/remote IP that hasn't been added to trusthost
  • Branch office without VPN where the FortiGate is administered from a public WAN IP
  • MSP technician administering customer FortiGate over the internet without jump host
  • CGNAT mobile-carrier IP used by a real on-call admin
  • Internal automation/health-check tool authenticating with the default account during migration
Suppression filter
| where SourceIP !in (dynamic(["<known_admin_home_ip>","<msp_jump_host>"])) and DeviceExternalID !startswith "LAB-"
Response runbook
1. Triage: Confirm the SourceIP is unfamiliar — check ASN, geolocation, and historical FortiGate auth log for prior successful logins from that IP for the account. Pull SSL VPN session state and any concurrent config writes by the same user. 2. Contain: Immediately terminate the session ('execute vpn ssl-vpn del-tunnel <user>' / 'execute sys logout admin'), rotate the password, disable the default account if not strictly required, restrict 'trusthost' on the admin profile to known management IPs, and force PBKDF2 rehash by re-saving the password (per FortiOS 7.2.11+/7.4.8/7.6.1 behaviour). 3. Hunt: Diff the FortiGate running-config against last known-good (look for new admin users, new SSL VPN portal users, mirrored interfaces, sniffer profiles, packet-capture rules, or modified Authd LDAP/RADIUS pointers that would enable traffic interception per the FortiBleed passive-monitoring stage). Search CommonSecurityLog for the same external IP hitting any other appliance.
let DefaultAdmins = dynamic(["admin","administrator","fortinet","maintainer","diag","super_admin","prof_admin","guest","sysadmin"]);
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DeviceVendor =~ "Fortinet" and DeviceProduct in~ ("Fortigate","FortiGate")
| where Activity has_any ("login","ssl vpn tunnel up","admin login successful","ssl-login-success") or DeviceEventClassID in ("32001","0100032001","0102043009")
| where EventOutcome in~ ("success","allowed","permit") or DeviceAction in~ ("login","login_success","ssl-login-success","tunnel-up")
| where tolower(SourceUserName) in (DefaultAdmins) or DestinationHostName in (DefaultAdmins)
| where ipv4_is_private(SourceIP) == false and isnotempty(SourceIP)
| project TimeGenerated, FortiGate = DeviceExternalID, FortiGateProduct = DeviceProduct, FortiGateHost = DestinationHostName, SourceIP, SourceUserName, DestinationHostName, Activity, DeviceAction, DeviceEventClassID, Message
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: FortiGate Successful Login With Default Admin Account From External IP

FortiGate config change within 10 minutes of admin login from a new external IP AIActions on Objectives Medium
Joins a successful FortiGate admin login from an external/never-seen IP with a configuration write event by the same admin within 10 minutes — the FortiBleed post-compromise pattern where the attacker logs in with a stuffed credential and immediately enables packet capture or mirrors traffic to begin passive credential harvesting. Rationale: Article specifies the post-compromise behaviour: 'Once access is obtained, they passively monitor network traffic going through the devices to collect additional credentials'. This requires CLI config changes (sniffer profiles, packet-capture, mirroring, modified Authd) immediately after login. CISA recommendation explicitly calls for reviewing logs for 'unauthorized configuration changes'. Cross-checked Arctic Wolf write-up describing the same two-stage credential-harvest flow. Cross-checked against: • https://www.ncsc.gov.uk/news/global-credential-stuffing-campaign-fortinet • https://arcticwolf.com/resources/blog/ • https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/alerts
ATT&CKT1556 T1098 T1078.001 T1040
Data sourcesAuthentication Change
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Network engineer doing a legitimate change-window push during maintenance, signing in from a home IP
  • Vendor-led troubleshooting session where Fortinet TAC walks the admin through 'diag sniffer packet' from a remote support session
  • FortiManager-driven config push misattributed when admin recently logged in from external IP
  • Net-new appliance commissioning where the first admin login + initial config build is expected
  • Legitimate enable of session-export/syslog destination at the same time as a routine login
Suppression filter
| where SourceIP !in (dynamic(["<change_window_jump_host>","<fortinet_tac_ip>"])) and CfgActivity !has_any ("backup","firmware","snmp-community")
Response runbook
1. Triage: For each match, isolate the exact CLI commands written — pull the full Message and any DeviceCustomString fields, and check whether the change touched 'sniffer', 'mirror', 'diagnose sniffer packet', 'config user', 'config system admin', 'config system replacemsg', or LDAP/RADIUS authentication-server pointers. Confirm the SourceIP is genuinely unfamiliar for that admin user (compare to last 30 days). 2. Contain: Roll back the suspicious config diff via FortiManager or `execute restore config` to the last known-good revision; terminate all admin/SSL VPN sessions; rotate all admin passwords; remove any newly-created admin/local-user accounts; disable interfaces in promiscuous/mirror mode added in the window. 3. Hunt: For the changed FortiGate, search CommonSecurityLog over the prior 30d for outbound traffic from the firewall management VRF to attacker infrastructure, search SSL VPN auth logs for any accounts whose credentials may have been sniffed, and across all FortiGate fle
let LookbackHrs = 7d;
let WindowSec = 600;
let Logins = CommonSecurityLog
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackHrs)
    | where DeviceVendor =~ "Fortinet" and DeviceProduct in~ ("Fortigate","FortiGate")
    | where (Activity has_any ("admin login successful","login","ssl vpn tunnel up") or DeviceEventClassID in ("32001","0100032001","0102043009"))
    | where EventOutcome in~ ("success","allowed") or DeviceAction in~ ("login","login_success","tunnel-up")
    | where ipv4_is_private(SourceIP) == false and isnotempty(SourceIP)
    | project LoginTime = TimeGenerated, FortiGate = DeviceExternalID, FortiGateHost = DestinationHostName,
              AdminUser = coalesce(SourceUserName, DestinationHostName), SourceIP;
let ConfigChanges = CommonSecurityLog
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackHrs)
    | where DeviceVendor =~ "Fortinet" and DeviceProduct in~ ("Fortigate","FortiGate")
    | where Activity has_any ("configuration","cfg","edit","config change","set","sniffer","packet-capture","diagnose sniffer") or DeviceEventClassID in ("44546","0100044546","44548","0100044548")
    | project CfgTime = TimeGenerated, FortiGate = DeviceExternalID, FortiGateHost = DestinationHostName,
              AdminUser = coalesce(SourceUserName, DestinationHostName), CfgMessage = Message, CfgActivity = Activity;
Logins
| join kind=inner ConfigChanges on FortiGate, AdminUser
| where CfgTime between (LoginTime .. LoginTime + WindowSec * 1s)
| extend DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', CfgTime, LoginTime)
| project LoginTime, CfgTime, DelaySec, FortiGate, FortiGateHost, AdminUser, SourceIP, CfgActivity, CfgMessage
| order by LoginTime desc
APPLICATION
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count min(_time) as login_time values(Authentication.src) as login_src from datamodel=Authentication where Authentication.action="success" Authentication.app IN ("fortigate","fortios") by Authentication.user Authentication.dest _time span=1s | `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)` | join type=inner user dest [| tstats summariesonly=true count as cfg_changes min(_time) as cfg_time values(All_Changes.object) as objects values(All_Changes.command) as commands from datamodel=Change where All_Changes.change_type="configuration" All_Changes.dest_category="network_device" by All_Changes.user All_Changes.dest _time span=1s | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Changes)` | rename user as user dest as dest] | where cfg_time >= login_time AND cfg_time <= login_time + 600 | eval delay_sec=cfg_time-login_time | search login_src!="10.0.0.0/8" login_src!="172.16.0.0/12" login_src!="192.168.0.0/16" | table login_time, cfg_time, delay_sec, user, dest, login_src, commands, objects
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as login_time values(Authentication.src) as login_src from datamodel=Authentication where Authentication.action="success" Authentication.app IN ("fortigate","fortios") by Authentication.user Authentication.dest _time span=1s | `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)` | join type=inner user dest [| tstats summariesonly=false count as cfg_changes min(_time) as cfg_time values(All_Changes.object) as objects values(All_Changes.command) as commands from datamodel=Change where All_Changes.change_type="configuration" All_Changes.dest_category="network_device" by All_Changes.user All_Changes.dest _time span=1s | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Changes)` | rename user as user dest as dest] | where cfg_time >= login_time AND cfg_time <= login_time + 600 | eval delay_sec=cfg_time-login_time | search login_src!="10.0.0.0/8" login_src!="172.16.0.0/12" login_src!="192.168.0.0/16" | table login_time, cfg_time, delay_sec, user, dest, login_src, commands, objects
Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs Actions on Objectives High
Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies SQLite from Chrome/Edge/Firefox.
ATT&CKT1539 T1555.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\", @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\", @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType

// ASIM ImFileEvent — covers MDE, Sysmon, AuditD, Defender for Cloud, etc.
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)

                                  @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\",

| where TargetFileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,

Node.js spawns /bin/sh -c with allowlist-prefix + shell metacharacter (CVE-2026-54051) AIExploitation High
Hunts the exploitation pattern for the Network-AI v<5.9.1 sandbox bypass: the Node.js orchestrator process spawning /bin/sh -c with an allowlisted token (git/npm/node/yarn/pnpm) followed by a shell metacharacter (;, &&, ||). This is the exact runtime signature of CVE-2026-54051's command-injection where SandboxPolicy.isCommandAllowed glob-matches the full string while ShellExecutor.execute hands it to /bin/sh -c. Rationale: Pivots on the exact two-part bug from the article: (a) parent is `node` (the Network-AI orchestrator runtime), (b) child is `sh`/`bash`/`dash` with `-c`, (c) command line carries both an allowlist-prefix token (`git `, `npm `, `node `, `yarn `, `pnpm ` — the wildcard allow patterns called out in Impact) AND a shell metacharacter that the regex glob (^git .*$) silently permits. PoC payload `git status; id > marker` lands on this. Cross-checked against the GHSA advisory text and the patch notes for v5.9.1 (commit 379f776) which explicitly reject `; & | $ ` ( ) < > { }` metacharacters. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-qw6v-5fcf-5666
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1190 T1068
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer using Network-AI / similar agent runtime locally and intentionally chaining commands in a permitted task (treat as TP-for-policy and have devs scope the allowlist down)
  • CI build steps where a Node.js wrapper invokes a shell with `git rev-parse HEAD; git log --oneline` style commands
  • Internal automation tooling that legitimately uses `node script.js` to orchestrate `sh -c 'npm install && npm test'`
  • Containerized entrypoint scripts where node spawns sh to run `git pull && npm ci`
  • Husky / lefthook git-hook runners that node-spawn sh to chain hook commands
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("husky", "lefthook", "npm run ", "yarn run ") and ProcessCommandLine has "&&" and not (ProcessCommandLine has_any (";", "||")))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full `ProcessCommandLine` and walk the tree — is the parent `node` running the `network-ai` package (check loaded modules / node_modules/network-ai/package.json version)? Confirm version < 5.9.1. 2) Contain: isolate the host; freeze the agent runtime (kill the node PID and its children); preserve `/tmp/nai-poc-*` style scratch dirs for forensics; rotate any credentials/SSH keys/tokens reachable from the orchestrator process's environment. 3) Hunt: pivot on the AccountName/DeviceName for the prior 30 days to find earlier exploitation; sweep for outbound network connections from the node PID; check for marker-file writes (e.g. PWNED-*.txt) and any new persistence (cron, systemd units, ~/.ssh/authorized_keys). Inventory all hosts running network-ai < 5.9.1 and accelerate upgrade.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "node"
| where FileName in~ ("sh", "bash", "dash")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "-c"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any (";", "&&", "||")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("git ", "npm ", "node ", "yarn ", "pnpm ")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName has "node"
| where ActingProcessName in~ ("sh", "bash", "dash")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "-c"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any (";", "&&", "||")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("git ", "npm ", "node ", "yarn ", "pnpm ")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
