FortiGate SSL VPN successful login after credential-stuffing burst (FortiBleed confirmed compromise) AIExploitation High
Confirms an actual FortiBleed compromise by correlating: a burst of SSL VPN failures from a source IP, immediately followed by a *successful* SSL VPN login from the same source IP on the same FortiGate within 1 hour. This is the single highest-fidelity signal that a leaked credential pair from the 73,932 exposed creds has actually worked. Rationale: Diachenko's research describes ~1.16 B SSL VPN authentication attempts as the harvesting mechanism; the only way to know a leaked plaintext credential pair actually validates is the failure→success transition from the same SourceIP on the same FortiGate. 1-hour window and ≥10 prior fails distinguish from typo-then-correct password retries. Cross-checked against: • https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1078/ • https://docs.fortinet.com/document/fortigate/7.4.0/fortios-log-reference
ATT&CKT1078 T1110.004 T1133
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • User forgot password, fails 10+ times, then succeeds after retrieving it
  • FortiClient mobile profile rotating expired token then re-auth succeeds
  • Help-desk validating new credentials by intentionally failing then succeeding
  • Pen-test engagement that ends with valid credentials being used
  • Account using stale cached creds across multiple devices, finally syncing
Suppression filter
and SuccessUser !in (dynamic(["<HELPDESK_TEST_ACCT>", "<PENTEST_ACCT>"]))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm SuccessUser identity, geolocate SourceIP, and verify whether the user is currently logged in elsewhere (impossible-travel check via SigninLogs). Treat as compromise unless the user confirms in-person they were locked-out then logged in. 2) Contain: immediately terminate the SSL VPN session on the FortiGate (`diagnose vpn ssl del-tunnel <user>`), reset the user's password, revoke the VPN session token, force MFA re-enrolment, and add SourceIP to the WAN block-list per CISA. 3) Hunt: pull all post-tunnel internal connections sourced from the SSL VPN-assigned IP for the past 7 d — look for RDP/SMB lateral movement, AD recon (LDAP/Kerberos), and config-file exfil; check Hudson Rock's FortiBleed lookup tool to confirm the device's credentials were in the leaked dataset.
let Window = 1h;
let Failures = CommonSecurityLog
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
    | where DeviceVendor =~ "Fortinet"
    | where Activity has "ssl-login-fail" 
        or DeviceEventClassID in ("0101039426", "39426")
        or Message has_any ("ssl-login-fail", "sslvpn_login_fail")
    | summarize FailCount = count(), 
                FirstFail = min(TimeGenerated), 
                LastFail = max(TimeGenerated),
                FailedUsers = make_set(SourceUserName, 25)
            by SourceIP, DeviceName
    | where FailCount >= 10;
let Successes = CommonSecurityLog
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
    | where DeviceVendor =~ "Fortinet"
    | where Activity has "ssl-login-success" 
        or DeviceEventClassID in ("0101039425", "39425")
        or Message has_any ("ssl-login-success", "SSL tunnel established", "sslvpn_login_success")
    | project SuccessTime = TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DeviceName, SuccessUser = SourceUserName, SuccessMessage = Message;
Failures
| join kind=inner Successes on SourceIP, DeviceName
| where SuccessTime between (FirstFail .. LastFail + Window)
| project FirstFail, LastFail, SuccessTime, DelayMin = datetime_diff('minute', SuccessTime, LastFail),
          SourceIP, DeviceName, FailCount, FailedUsers, SuccessUser, SuccessMessage
| order by SuccessTime desc
source:fortinet @evt.name:(ssl-login-fail OR ssl-login-success)

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

AutoJack: How a single page can RCE the host running your AI agent

Microsoft Security Blog
2026-06-19 9 use cases 7 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

AutoJack is a novel exploit chain showing how a single malicious webpage can turn an AI browsing agent into a remote code execution vector on the host machine. By abusing trust in localhost, missing authentication, and unsafe parameter handling, attackers can trigger arbitrary process execution through AutoGen Studio’s MCP WebSocket. The research highlights a broader pattern - when agents can browse untrusted content and access local services, traditional boundaries like localhost are no longer secure. Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Headless browser / Playwright child of autogenstudio connecting to localhost:8081 · [LLM] HTTP request to /api/mcp/ws/ endpoint with server_params query parameter (AutoJack payload) · [LLM] AutoGen agent external web fetch followed by localhost MCP port connection (time-correlation)
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] AutoGen Studio Python parent spawning shell / LOLBin child (StdioServerParams RCE) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — AutoJack: How a single page can RCE the host running your AI agent
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Headless browser / Playwright child of autogenstudio connecting to localhost:8081 AIDelivery Medium
Hunts for the AutoJack network primitive: an agent-controlled headless browser (Playwright / MultimodalWebSurfer / Chromium headless) opening a connection to 127.0.0.1 on AutoGen Studio's MCP WebSocket port (8081 by default). This is the localhost-trust-boundary crossing the article describes — a browser process whose ancestor is the Python autogenstudio runtime is exactly the shape an external page-driven hijack produces. Rationale: Anchors on (a) the exact MCP WebSocket port 8081 named in the article's Figure 1 (`ws://localhost:8081/api/mcp/ws/`), (b) the loopback addresses 127.0.0.1/::1 that the Origin allowlist trusts (Issue 1), and (c) the agent-spawned headless browser process tree (Playwright / MultimodalWebSurfer) the article explicitly calls out as the trust-boundary defeater. The join on DeviceId/DvcHostname binds the network event to the agent-process context. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/microsoft/autogen/commit/b047730 • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1190/
ATT&CKT1190 T1559
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Endpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer manually pointing a Playwright test at a local FastAPI app on port 8000/8081
  • AutoGen Studio legitimate use — the dev themselves prompts the agent to fetch a benign page that happens to call back to the MCP
  • Local frontend dev servers (Vite/Next.js) that proxy through Chromium DevTools on 8080
  • Pytest-playwright suites in CI running against a co-located backend
Suppression filter
| where not (BrowserCmd has "--user-data-dir=" and BrowserCmd has_any ("\\AppData\\Local\\ms-playwright","\\node_modules\\playwright") and AgentParentCmd has_any ("pytest","playwright test","npm test"))
Response runbook
1) Triage — pull the BrowserCmd and AgentParentCmd; if `--remote-debugging-port` is present and the agent parent has any `MultimodalWebSurfer`/`fetch_webpage_tool`/`autogen_agentchat` token, treat as in-scope. Pull DeviceProcessEvents for the BrowserPid's children in the next 60s. 2) Contain — kill the python.exe ancestor PID; block 8081 on the host firewall; isolate the device in MDE if any non-browser child spawned. 3) Hunt — pivot on AccountName for other agent-host pairs; check DeviceNetworkEvents for the same browser process reaching external URLs immediately before the loopback hit (the page that drove the hijack) and submit those URLs to URL detonation.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let AgentBrowsers = DeviceProcessEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where FileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","chromium.exe","playwright.exe","headless_shell.exe","node.exe")
    | where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python.exe","pythonw.exe","autogenstudio.exe")
         or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("playwright","--remote-debugging-port","MultimodalWebSurfer","autogen","headless")
    | project ProcTime = Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, AccountName,
              BrowserProc = FileName, BrowserCmd = ProcessCommandLine,
              AgentParent = InitiatingProcessFileName, AgentParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
              BrowserPid = ProcessId;
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where RemoteIP in ("127.0.0.1","::1")
| where RemotePort in (8081, 8080, 8000)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| join kind=inner AgentBrowsers on DeviceId
| where Timestamp between (ProcTime .. ProcTime + 2h)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, BrowserProc, BrowserCmd,
          AgentParent, AgentParentCmd, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let AgentBrowsers = ImProcessCreate
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where ActingProcessName has_any ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","chromium.exe","playwright.exe","headless_shell.exe","node.exe")
    | where ParentProcessName has_any ("python.exe","pythonw.exe","autogenstudio.exe")
         or ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("playwright","--remote-debugging-port","MultimodalWebSurfer","autogen","headless")
    | project ProcTime = TimeGenerated, DvcHostname,
              BrowserProc = ActingProcessName, BrowserCmd = ActingProcessCommandLine,
              AgentParent = ParentProcessName, AgentParentCmd = ParentProcessCommandLine,
              BrowserPid = ActingProcessId;
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where DstIpAddr in ("127.0.0.1","::1")
| where DstPortNumber in (8081, 8080, 8000)
| join kind=inner AgentBrowsers on DvcHostname
| where TimeGenerated between (ProcTime .. ProcTime + 2h)
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, BrowserProc, BrowserCmd,
          AgentParent, AgentParentCmd, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, NetworkProtocol, Url
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:3 @DestinationIp:(127.0.0.1 OR ::1) @DestinationPort:(8081 OR 8080 OR 8000) @Image:(*\\chrome.exe OR *\\Chrome.exe OR *\\msedge.exe OR *\\MSEdge.exe OR *\\chromium.exe OR *\\playwright.exe OR *\\headless_shell.exe OR *\\node.exe) (@ParentImage:(*\\python.exe OR *\\Python.exe OR *\\pythonw.exe OR *\\autogenstudio.exe) OR @CommandLine:(*MultimodalWebSurfer* OR *playwright* OR *--remote-debugging-port* OR *autogen*))
#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4 (RemoteAddressIP4="127.0.0.1" OR RemoteAddressIP4="::1") RemotePort=/^(8081|8080|8000)$/ ContextImageFileName=/\\(chrome|msedge|chromium|playwright|headless_shell|node)\.exe$/i
| join({#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ParentBaseFileName=/^(python|pythonw|autogenstudio)\.exe$/i ImageFileName=/\\(chrome|msedge|chromium|playwright|headless_shell|node)\.exe$/i}, field=[aid, ContextProcessId], key=[aid, TargetProcessId])
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, RemoteAddressIP4, RemotePort], function=count())

| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Processes.process) as cmdline values(Processes.parent_process_name) as parent from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","chromium.exe","playwright.exe","headless_shell.exe","node.exe") AND (Processes.parent_process_name IN ("python.exe","pythonw.exe","autogenstudio.exe") OR Processes.process=*MultimodalWebSurfer* OR Processes.process=*playwright* OR Processes.process=*--remote-debugging-port*) by host Processes.process_name Processes.parent_process_name Processes.user | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | join type=inner host [| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where All_Traffic.dest IN ("127.0.0.1","::1") AND All_Traffic.dest_port IN (8081,8080,8000) by host All_Traffic.dest All_Traffic.dest_port | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`] | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
AutoGen Studio Python parent spawning shell / LOLBin child (StdioServerParams RCE) AIExploitation High
Hunts the AutoJack execution primitive: a python.exe / pythonw.exe / autogenstudio.exe process spawning calc.exe, powershell.exe, cmd.exe, bash.exe, or any LOLBin as a direct child. The article's Code Block 2 shows `stdio_client(StdioServerParams(...))` will execute `command` and `args` from the URL verbatim — the resulting child has the autogenstudio runtime as its parent process. Rationale: The article's Code Block 3 shows the exact payload (`{"command":"calc.exe","args":[],...}`) being handed to `stdio_client(...)` — the spawned process inherits the autogenstudio uvicorn/FastAPI Python parent. The combined parent-process + parent-cmdline anchor (autogenstudio token) + child LOLBin set is high-fidelity because legitimate AutoGen tool plumbing spawns specific MCP server binaries (npx, uvx) — not raw shells / calc. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/microsoft/autogen/commit/b047730 • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1190/
ATT&CKT1059.001 T1059.003 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer running an AutoGen tool that legitimately wraps a PowerShell helper (rare but plausible for code-execution-tool prototypes)
  • Jupyter/IPython embedded in autogenstudio launching cmd.exe for a `!shell` cell
  • MCP server developer using `bash -c` as the configured command for a custom MCP server during local testing
  • PyInstaller-packed autogenstudio launching the LOLBin as a legitimate startup helper
Suppression filter
| where not (ChildCmd has_any ("npx","uvx") and ParentCmd has "--mcp-server")
Response runbook
1) Triage — read ChildCmd. If it's `calc.exe` with no args, treat as proof-of-concept demonstration; if it's powershell/cmd/bash with a download/encoded payload, treat as full RCE. Capture grandchildren of the LOLBin and any DeviceFileEvents writes by that PID. 2) Contain — kill the autogenstudio Python PID and its tree; disconnect host; rotate any credentials available to the developer account. 3) Hunt — pivot on AccountName for prior loopback DeviceNetworkEvents to ports 8000/8080/8081; pivot on DeviceName for the page URL the browsing-agent fetched immediately before this spawn (likely the malicious page hosting the JS that opened the WebSocket).
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python.exe","pythonw.exe","autogenstudio.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("autogenstudio","autogen_agentchat","autogen_ext","ui.app","uvicorn","mcp")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","bash.exe","wsl.exe","calc.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","certutil.exe","bitsadmin.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          ParentImage = InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          ChildImage = FolderPath,
          ChildCmd = ProcessCommandLine,
          SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("python.exe","pythonw.exe","autogenstudio.exe")
| where ParentProcessCommandLine has_any ("autogenstudio","autogen_agentchat","autogen_ext","ui.app","uvicorn","mcp")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","bash.exe","wsl.exe","calc.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","certutil.exe","bitsadmin.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername,
          ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine,
          ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

HTTP request to /api/mcp/ws/ endpoint with server_params query parameter (AutoJack payload) AIDelivery High
Targets the AutoJack payload signature in any HTTP/WebSocket telemetry: a request to the path `/api/mcp/ws/` carrying a `server_params=` query parameter. The article's Code Block 2 shows this is the literal endpoint the malicious page calls to deliver the base64-JSON StdioServerParams blob. Hunts proxy / WAF / browser history / packet capture wherever it lands. Rationale: The path `/api/mcp/ws/` and query parameter name `server_params` come verbatim from the article's Code Block 2 (router definition + `websocket.query_params.get("server_params")`). This pair is essentially zero-FP outside the AutoJack chain — it isn't a generic WebSocket pattern; it's the AutoGen Studio MCP route signature. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/microsoft/autogen/commit/b047730
ATT&CKT1190 T1505.003
Data sourcesWeb.Web Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • AutoGen Studio developer manually browsing /api/mcp/ws/?server_params=... during their own debugging (pivot on the source IP — should be the local dev box)
  • Internal red-team / purple-team replay of the AutoJack PoC against a deliberately-vulnerable test instance
  • Static code scanner / SAST product that crawls and probes localhost endpoints
  • Security researcher running the published PoC in a lab
Response runbook
1) Triage — base64-decode the server_params value (everything after `server_params=` up to next `&`). If it deserialises to a JSON with `command` and `args` keys, the chain is confirmed. Identify the source IP of the request and the user-agent. 2) Contain — block the source IP at the perimeter; if internal, isolate the originating host; force-upgrade any AutoGen Studio dev install older than commit b047730. 3) Hunt — pivot on AccountName/DeviceName for DeviceProcessEvents children of python.exe in the next 60s; pivot on the decoded `command` value to find prior runs of the same payload across the fleet.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where isnotempty(RemoteUrl)
| where RemoteUrl has "/api/mcp/ws/"
   and RemoteUrl has "server_params="
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Url has "/api/mcp/ws/"
   and Url has "server_params="
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber,
          Url, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, HttpRequestHeaderReferer
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: AutoGen Studio MCP WebSocket Hijack URL Pattern (AutoJack)
id: 7e4f9b2c-1a8d-4e6f-b3c2-9d5a8e1f3b67
description: Detects HTTP / WebSocket requests carrying the AutoGen Studio MCP WebSocket hijack URL pattern — path /api/mcp/ws/ with a server_params query parameter that base64-decodes to StdioServerParams executed verbatim.
references:

detection:
  selection:
    cs-uri-stem|contains: '/api/mcp/ws/'
    cs-uri-query|contains: 'server_params='
  condition: selection
level: high
(source:windows.sysmon OR source:cloudtrail OR source:nginx OR source:apache) (@http.url:*\/api\/mcp\/ws\/* OR @url:*\/api\/mcp\/ws\/*) (@http.url:*server_params=* OR @url:*server_params=*)
#event_simpleName=DnsRequest OR #event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4 OR #event_simpleName=HttpRequest
| regex("/api/mcp/ws/", field=DomainName) OR regex("/api/mcp/ws/", field=HttpUrl) OR regex("/api/mcp/ws/", field=Url)
| regex("server_params=", field=HttpUrl) OR regex("server_params=", field=Url)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, Url], function=count())

| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Web.url) as urls values(Web.src) as src from datamodel=Web.Web where Web.url="*/api/mcp/ws/*" AND Web.url="*server_params=*" by host Web.dest Web.user | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
AutoGen agent external web fetch followed by localhost MCP port connection (time-correlation) AIDelivery Medium
Detects the full AutoJack delivery shape: an AutoGen agent process (python parent running MultimodalWebSurfer/Playwright/fetch_webpage_tool) makes an outbound HTTPS request to an external public IP, then within 60 seconds the same host opens a connection to 127.0.0.1:8081. This is the article's Figure 1 chain end-to-end — external page fetched → JS in the page calls the localhost MCP endpoint. Rationale: Implements the time-window-correlation pattern against the exact AutoJack chain from Figure 1: external page render → loopback MCP WebSocket on 8081. Anchors on public-then-loopback within 60s by the same agent-class process on the same host. The 60s window matches the article's no-user-interaction click-to-hijack latency. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/microsoft/autogen/commit/b047730
ATT&CKT1199 T1190 T1204.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer iterating on an AutoGen tool that legitimately fetches public docs then hits a local MCP test server
  • Chromium DevTools auto-attach reaching localhost:9222 right after a page load (different port, but a CDP-on-8081 misconfig could trip)
  • Local LLM gateway (Ollama / LMStudio) on 8080 polled from the same browser session that just fetched a model card
  • Web-app dev with frontend on localhost:8080 fetching CDN assets externally
Suppression filter
| where not (ExternalUrl has_any ("github.com","pypi.org","huggingface.co","openai.com","anthropic.com") and AgentCmd has_any ("pip install","pip download"))
Response runbook
1) Triage — pull the ExternalUrl that preceded the loopback hit. Detonate it (URL sandbox / urlscan) and inspect for inline JavaScript that opens `new WebSocket("ws://localhost:8081/api/mcp/ws/?server_params=...")`. 2) Contain — if the URL is non-benign, block the domain, isolate the host, kill the autogenstudio Python PID. 3) Hunt — pivot on the ExternalUrl across the fleet for other agents that fetched it; pivot on DeviceName for DeviceProcessEvents children of python.exe spawned within 5s after LoopbackTime (the actual RCE child).
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let WindowSeconds = 60;
let ExternalFetch = DeviceNetworkEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where RemotePort in (80, 443, 8443)
    | where RemoteIPType == "Public"
    | where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python.exe","pythonw.exe","chrome.exe","msedge.exe","chromium.exe","playwright.exe","headless_shell.exe","node.exe")
    | where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("autogenstudio","autogen","MultimodalWebSurfer","fetch_webpage","playwright","--remote-debugging-port")
         or InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("python.exe","pythonw.exe","autogenstudio.exe")
    | project ExternalTime = Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName,
              ExternalUrl = RemoteUrl, ExternalIP = RemoteIP,
              AgentProc = InitiatingProcessFileName, AgentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine;
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where RemoteIP in ("127.0.0.1","::1")
| where RemotePort in (8081, 8080, 8000)
| join kind=inner ExternalFetch on DeviceId
| where Timestamp between (ExternalTime .. ExternalTime + WindowSeconds * 1s)
| extend DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ExternalTime)
| project ExternalTime, LoopbackTime = Timestamp, DelaySec,
          DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, ExternalUrl, ExternalIP,
          AgentProc, AgentCmd, LoopbackPort = RemotePort
| order by ExternalTime desc
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let WindowSeconds = 60;
let ExternalFetch = ImNetworkSession
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where DstPortNumber in (80, 443, 8443)
    | where not(ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr)) and DstIpAddr !in ("127.0.0.1","::1")
    | project ExternalTime = TimeGenerated, DvcHostname,
              ExternalUrl = Url, ExternalIP = DstIpAddr;
let AgentProcs = ImProcessCreate
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where ActingProcessName has_any ("python.exe","pythonw.exe","chrome.exe","msedge.exe","chromium.exe","playwright.exe","headless_shell.exe","node.exe")
    | where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("autogenstudio","autogen","MultimodalWebSurfer","fetch_webpage","playwright")
         or ParentProcessName has_any ("python.exe","pythonw.exe","autogenstudio.exe")
    | distinct DvcHostname;
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where DstIpAddr in ("127.0.0.1","::1")

title: PsExec / SMB Lateral Movement Tooling Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d03
status: experimental
description: |
    PsExec, paexec, smbexec, csexec, remcom — admin-grade tooling that
    pivots over SMB. Pair with `wmic /node:` for the full cluster.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1021/002/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1569/002/

    - attack.lateral-movement
    - attack.execution

    category: process_creation
    product: windows

Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code.
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] GentleKiller / HexKiller / ThrottleBlood / HavocKiller binary hash hit · [LLM] BYOVD vulnerable-driver service install impersonating Kaspersky/Valorant/Javelin/WatchDog · [LLM] Mass termination of 48-vendor EDR/AV process set within short window · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
GentleKiller / HexKiller / ThrottleBlood / HavocKiller binary hash hit AIInstallation High
Alerts on execution or file-write of any binary whose SHA1 matches the 20 ESET-published GentleKiller/HexKiller/ThrottleBlood/HavocKiller hashes tied to Gentlemen RaaS. These hashes were enumerated by ESET across at least 8 GentleKiller variants and three external EDR-killers. A hit means an in-scope ransomware-precursor binary touched the host and pre-encryption defense-disablement is imminent. Rationale: Uses the 20 SHA1 hashes attributed by ESET (the only researchers cited) to GentleKiller/HexKiller/ThrottleBlood/HavocKiller, covering both execution (ProcessEvents) and on-disk drop (FileEvents). The hash list is the article's most concrete IOC set and the only one that gives an unambiguous true-positive verdict.
ATT&CKT1562.001 T1068
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Reverse-engineer or malware analyst intentionally detonating sample on a lab host
  • SOC purple-team or BAS tool replaying the same hashes in a controlled test
  • Threat-intel ingestion pipeline writing the binary to a hashed quarantine path
  • Backup or forensic-imaging tools copying a previously-detected sample
Suppression filter
| where not (DeviceName has_any ("malware-lab","sandbox-","-detonation") or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"\AVAnalysis\", @"\Forensics\"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE — confirm the device is a production endpoint, not the malware-analysis lab; pull full ProcessEvents/FileEvents tree for the matching SHA1 in the prior 60 minutes; identify the initiating user and parent binary (typical Gentlemen chain has the killer dropped after initial RDP / RMM intrusion). 2) CONTAIN — isolate the host via Defender or Falcon network containment; expire all cached credentials for the logged-on user; query EDR for any service stops on security products (Defender/CrowdStrike/SentinelOne) in the last 24h on this host. 3) HUNT — pivot on the parent process hash and the dropping account across the fleet; query for the same hashes anywhere in the estate (file-events) and for vulnerable-driver names (see UC2) since Gentlemen affiliates often pre-stage drivers on multiple hosts before encryption.
let GentlemenSHA1 = dynamic(["8AE6BD18B129061F63642531F1B684CF0383C75D","BA914FE77B177B45799403B16DD14765C510A074","D605994FC72A2BB59B5CFB1624A1B9170ECA73A2","B0B912A3FD1C05D72080848EC4C92880004021A1","5AA3124E5C4921E5EDFC60133B5D71DA21B07DA3","7556AE58C215B8245A43F764F0676C7A8F0FDD1A","331879F5EEC8892BBD896F90BDBB1BAD0BF63BD6","F11AEBCCB9A86A7E2E653F90BAEC697F233C255F","EF9CD06683159397F099CAA244E94E6EAAD96EBA","711EF221526997039E804A18DB9647C91680BBE2","68FEC379F2AE76C3D2CE913F7BE650CEA1D06990","A11EE9CDC59E5CAA59AEFD27B30D104F3AD68E62","96F0DBF52AED0AFD43E44500116B04B674F7358E","2F86898528C6CAB3540C486A9BFAA0C029B73950","9AD51AD97C01E97AB59214116740785E0F6320A8","A19117175DBC9BA4D23B5DCE8415E299A2E32192","12500F6C87CE62712A0ED6652C57468D15C14223","D29670E684E40DDC89B47010C37CBC96737035B6","56BEE9DF5833A637F5C54D5911DF98B0812FE643","CF4D74DF17A91B4A36A2911B22AFEC5D8FA93A01"]);
let ProcHits = DeviceProcessEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
  | where SHA1 in~ (GentlemenSHA1) or InitiatingProcessSHA1 in~ (GentlemenSHA1)
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA1, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine;
let FileHits = DeviceFileEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
  | where SHA1 in~ (GentlemenSHA1) or InitiatingProcessSHA1 in~ (GentlemenSHA1)
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName=FileName, FolderPath, SHA1, ProcessCommandLine=InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine;
ProcHits | union FileHits | order by Timestamp desc
let GentlemenSHA1 = dynamic(["8AE6BD18B129061F63642531F1B684CF0383C75D","BA914FE77B177B45799403B16DD14765C510A074","D605994FC72A2BB59B5CFB1624A1B9170ECA73A2","B0B912A3FD1C05D72080848EC4C92880004021A1","5AA3124E5C4921E5EDFC60133B5D71DA21B07DA3","7556AE58C215B8245A43F764F0676C7A8F0FDD1A","331879F5EEC8892BBD896F90BDBB1BAD0BF63BD6","F11AEBCCB9A86A7E2E653F90BAEC697F233C255F","EF9CD06683159397F099CAA244E94E6EAAD96EBA","711EF221526997039E804A18DB9647C91680BBE2","68FEC379F2AE76C3D2CE913F7BE650CEA1D06990","A11EE9CDC59E5CAA59AEFD27B30D104F3AD68E62","96F0DBF52AED0AFD43E44500116B04B674F7358E","2F86898528C6CAB3540C486A9BFAA0C029B73950","9AD51AD97C01E97AB59214116740785E0F6320A8","A19117175DBC9BA4D23B5DCE8415E299A2E32192","12500F6C87CE62712A0ED6652C57468D15C14223","D29670E684E40DDC89B47010C37CBC96737035B6","56BEE9DF5833A637F5C54D5911DF98B0812FE643","CF4D74DF17A91B4A36A2911B22AFEC5D8FA93A01"]);
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where SHA1 in~ (GentlemenSHA1)
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine, SHA1, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine

BYOVD vulnerable-driver service install impersonating Kaspersky/Valorant/Javelin/WatchDog AIInstallation Medium
Hunts kernel-driver service creation where the service or ImagePath uses names GentleKiller variants impersonate — Kaspersky, Valorant (Riot), Javelin, WatchDog — but the driver file does NOT live under the legitimate vendor path. Catches the BYOVD step where Gentlemen registers a vulnerable driver under a security-product mask to obtain Ring 0. Rationale: Article explicitly lists Kaspersky / Valorant / Javelin / WatchDog as the four product names that GentleKiller variants impersonate, and ESET notes each variant ships a different vulnerable driver. Detecting the impersonated service-name + non-vendor path catches the BYOVD step regardless of which CVE driver the affiliate loads.
ATT&CKT1068 T1543.003 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Genuine Kaspersky AV reinstall from a non-standard custom installer path
  • Legit Valorant/Vanguard install on a corporate dev host (rare but happens on dual-use laptops)
  • Security-vendor IR tooling that registers a temporary kernel helper under a vendor-branded service name
  • Pen-test or BAS tool simulating a BYOVD install
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("msiexec.exe","setup.exe") and InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("explorer.exe") and InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$" and RegistryValueData has_any (@"\Kaspersky Lab\", @"\Riot Vanguard\"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE — pull the InitiatingProcess (who registered the service) and the driver file SHA256; cross-reference the SHA256 against loldrivers.io to confirm it is a known vulnerable driver; verify the legit vendor product is/isn't actually installed via DeviceTvmSoftwareInventory. 2) CONTAIN — stop and delete the rogue service (sc.exe delete <name>) before reboot; isolate the host; revoke the user session that wrote the registry value. 3) HUNT — pivot on the writing process across the fleet; search DeviceFileEvents for the driver SHA256 on every endpoint (Gentlemen pre-stages drivers across multiple hosts); check for any of the 20 hashes in UC1 on the same host in the prior 24h.
DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("RegistryValueSet","RegistryKeyCreated")
| where RegistryKey has @"\System\CurrentControlSet\Services\"
| where (RegistryValueName =~ "ImagePath" and RegistryValueData has_any ("kaspersky","valorant","vgk.sys","javelin","watchdog","wdog","wsdk"))
     or (RegistryKey has_any (@"\Services\kaspersky",@"\Services\valorant",@"\Services\vgk",@"\Services\javelin",@"\Services\watchdog",@"\Services\wdog") and RegistryValueName =~ "ImagePath")
| where not (RegistryValueData has_any (@"\Program Files\Kaspersky Lab\", @"\Program Files\Riot Vanguard\", @"\Program Files\Valorant\"))
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, RegistryKey, RegistryValueName, RegistryValueData, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessSHA1
| order by Timestamp desc
let ImpersonatedNames = dynamic(["kaspersky","valorant","vgk","javelin","watchdog","wdog","wsdk"]);
let LegitPaths = dynamic([@"\Program Files\Kaspersky Lab\", @"\Program Files\Riot Vanguard\", @"\Program Files\Valorant\"]);
Event
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Source == "Service Control Manager" and EventID == 7045
| extend ServiceName = tostring(parse_xml(EventData).EventData.Data[0])
| extend ImagePath = tostring(parse_xml(EventData).EventData.Data[1])
| extend ServiceType = tostring(parse_xml(EventData).EventData.Data[2])
| where ServiceType has "kernel" or ImagePath endswith ".sys"
| where tolower(ServiceName) has_any (ImpersonatedNames) or tolower(ImagePath) has_any (ImpersonatedNames)
| where not (ImagePath has_any (LegitPaths))
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ServiceName, ImagePath, ServiceType, User
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Themida/Enigma packed binary with security-vendor masquerade name from user-writable path AIDelivery Medium
Hunts process executions where the binary file name matches the security-vendor masks GentleKiller wears (Kaspersky, Valorant, Javelin, WatchDog), the binary runs from a user-writable directory (Temp, ProgramData, Public, Downloads), and the on-disk file is Themida/Enigma-packed. This catches GentleKiller variants where hash rotation has invalidated UC1 but the masquerade pattern is preserved. Rationale: Article calls out specifically that GentleKiller's 8 variants 'impersonate various legitimate security products, including Kaspersky, Valorant, Javelin, and WatchDog' and that the binaries are Themida/Enigma packed with stolen-but-invalid signatures. Anchoring on (impersonated name) ∧ (non-vendor path) survives hash rotation; signing-info anomaly is a useful tertiary signal.
ATT&CKT1036.005 T1027.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer extracting a vendor installer to %TEMP% for analysis or repackaging
  • Custom IT-deployment script staging Kaspersky installer in C:\ProgramData\Kaspersky_install\
  • Gamer running Valorant from a non-default user-profile install
  • Security researcher detonating packed samples in a Downloads folder
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("msiexec.exe","setup.exe","vc_redist.x64.exe") and InitiatingProcessAccountName endswith "$") and ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName !has_any ("Kaspersky","Riot Games")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE — extract the SHA256, the ProcessVersionInfo block, and the signing status from DeviceFileEvents; check whether the legitimate vendor product is installed elsewhere on the host (DeviceTvmSoftwareInventory) — if not, the masquerade is the whole point. 2) CONTAIN — kill the process, quarantine the binary, isolate the host if a kernel-driver service was also registered (correlate with UC2). 3) HUNT — search DeviceProcessEvents for the same binary by hash across the fleet; pivot on the dropping process to identify the upstream loader / initial-access vector; check FortiGate auth logs for the user given the article's note that Gentlemen targets FortiGate-configured environments.
let MasqNames = dynamic(["kaspersky","avp","avpui","valorant","vgc","vgk","javelin","watchdog","wdog"]);
let SuspectPaths = dynamic([@"\Users\Public\", @"\ProgramData\", @"\Windows\Temp\", @"\PerfLogs\", @"\AppData\Local\Temp\", @"\Downloads\"]);
let LegitPaths = dynamic([@"\Program Files\Kaspersky Lab\", @"\Program Files\Riot Vanguard\", @"\Program Files\Valorant\", @"\Program Files (x86)\Kaspersky Lab\"]);
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| extend FNameLow = tolower(FileName)
| where FNameLow has_any (MasqNames)
| where FolderPath has_any (SuspectPaths)
| where not (FolderPath has_any (LegitPaths))
| extend SignerSuspect = (ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName !has_any ("Kaspersky","Riot Games","Microsoft")) or isempty(ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, SHA1,
          ProcessCommandLine, ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName, ProcessVersionInfoProductName, ProcessVersionInfoOriginalFileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SignerSuspect
| order by Timestamp desc
let MasqNames = dynamic(["kaspersky","avp","avpui","valorant","vgc","vgk","javelin","watchdog","wdog"]);
let SuspectPaths = dynamic([@"\Users\Public\", @"\ProgramData\", @"\Windows\Temp\", @"\PerfLogs\", @"\AppData\Local\Temp\", @"\Downloads\"]);
let LegitPaths = dynamic([@"\Program Files\Kaspersky Lab\", @"\Program Files\Riot Vanguard\", @"\Program Files\Valorant\"]);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EventID == 4688
| extend FNameLow = tolower(NewProcessName)
| where FNameLow has_any (MasqNames)
| where FNameLow has_any (SuspectPaths)
| where not (FNameLow has_any (LegitPaths))
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Gentlemen GentleKiller Masquerade Binary from User-Writable Path
id: 9c3e8a7b-4b1a-4d62-8aa3-2f6d4b1c9a03
description: Detects execution of a binary whose name impersonates Kaspersky, Riot Valorant/Vanguard, Javelin or WatchDog from a user-writable directory (Temp/Public/ProgramData/Downloads) — the GentleKiller masquerade footprint when hashes have rotated.
references:
  - https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/gentlemen-ransomware-uses-multiple-edr-killers-to-disable-defenses/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/19
tags:
  - attack.t1036.005
  - attack.t1027.002
  - attack.defense_evasion
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_name:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\kaspersky.exe'
      - '\avp.exe'
      - '\avpui.exe'
      - '\valorant.exe'
      - '\vgc.exe'
      - '\vgk.exe'
      - '\javelin.exe'
      - '\watchdog.exe'
      - '\wdog.exe'
  selection_path:
    Image|contains:
      - '\Users\Public\'
      - '\ProgramData\'
      - '\Windows\Temp\'
      - '\PerfLogs\'
      - '\AppData\Local\Temp\'
      - '\Downloads\'
  filter_legit:
    Image|contains:
      - '\Program Files\Kaspersky Lab\'
      - '\Program Files\Riot Vanguard\'
      - '\Program Files\Valorant\'
  condition: selection_name and selection_path and not filter_legit
level: medium
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 (@Image:(*\\kaspersky.exe OR *\\Kaspersky.exe OR *\\KASPERSKY.exe OR *\\avp.exe OR *\\AVP.exe OR *\\avpui.exe OR *\\valorant.exe OR *\\Valorant.exe OR *\\VALORANT.exe OR *\\vgc.exe OR *\\VGC.exe OR *\\vgk.exe OR *\\VGK.exe OR *\\javelin.exe OR *\\Javelin.exe OR *\\watchdog.exe OR *\\WatchDog.exe OR *\\WATCHDOG.exe OR *\\wdog.exe)) AND (@Image:(*\\Users\\Public\\* OR *\\users\\public\\* OR *\\ProgramData\\* OR *\\programdata\\* OR *\\Windows\\Temp\\* OR *\\windows\\temp\\* OR *\\PerfLogs\\* OR *\\AppData\\Local\\Temp\\* OR *\\Downloads\\*)) -@Image:(*\\Program\ Files\\Kaspersky\ Lab\\* OR *\\Program\ Files\\Riot\ Vanguard\\* OR *\\Program\ Files\\Valorant\\*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 | ImageFileName=/\\(kaspersky|avp|avpui|valorant|vgc|vgk|javelin|watchdog|wdog)\.exe$/i | ImageFileName=/\\(Users\\Public|ProgramData|Windows\\Temp|PerfLogs|AppData\\Local\\Temp|Downloads)\\/i | NOT ImageFileName=/\\Program Files( \(x86\))?\\(Kaspersky Lab|Riot Vanguard|Valorant)\\/i | groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ImageFileName, SHA256HashData, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT

| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Processes.process) as cmdline values(Processes.parent_process_name) as parent values(Processes.process_hash) as hash from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name="kaspersky*" OR Processes.process_name="avp*" OR Processes.process_name="valorant*" OR Processes.process_name="vgc*" OR Processes.process_name="vgk*" OR Processes.process_name="javelin*" OR Processes.process_name="watchdog*" OR Processes.process_name="wdog*") (Processes.process_path="*\\Users\\*\\AppData\\Local\\Temp\\*" OR Processes.process_path="*\\ProgramData\\*" OR Processes.process_path="*\\Users\\Public\\*" OR Processes.process_path="*\\Users\\*\\Downloads\\*" OR Processes.process_path="*\\Windows\\Temp\\*" OR Processes.process_path="*\\Perflogs\\*") NOT (Processes.process_path="*\\Program Files\\Kaspersky Lab\\*" OR Processes.process_path="*\\Program Files\\Riot Vanguard\\*" OR Processes.process_path="*\\Program Files\\Valorant\\*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process_path | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Mass termination of 48-vendor EDR/AV process set within short window AIInstallation High
Detects when 10+ distinct security-vendor processes (Microsoft Defender, CrowdStrike, SentinelOne, Palo Alto, Sophos, Trend Micro, ESET, Bitdefender, McAfee/Trellix, Kaspersky) terminate on a single host within a 5-minute window — the unmistakable signature of GentleKiller's kernel-mode process-kill loop targeting ~400 processes across ~48 vendors. Independent of which BYOVD driver or hash variant was used. Rationale: Article states GentleKiller 'targets more than 400 processes associated with approximately 48 security vendors' including the named vendor list. Threshold of 10 distinct security-vendor processes dying in 5 min is well above legitimate uninstall/upgrade noise (one product = ~3-5 procs) and matches the kernel-mode kill-loop signature shared across all 8 variants + HexKiller/ThrottleBlood/HavocKiller.
ATT&CKT1562.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Bulk EDR migration day (uninstalling old agent + installing new) — usually scheduled & ticketed
  • SCCM/Intune deploying a corp-wide AV swap
  • Sysadmin troubleshooting a stuck EDR with multiple service restarts
  • Disk imaging / golden-image refresh wiping security stack pre-recapture
Suppression filter
| where not (DeviceName in~ (toscalar(DeviceTvmSoftwareInventory | where SoftwareName has_any ("CrowdStrike","SentinelOne","Defender for Endpoint") | where Timestamp between (ago(1h) .. now()) | summarize make_set(DeviceName))))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE — verify against the change/maintenance calendar that no scheduled EDR swap or migration is running on the host; pull DeviceProcessEvents for the 30 minutes before the kill cluster to identify the parent that initiated termination; check for any UC1 hash or UC2 driver service in the same window. 2) CONTAIN — network-isolate immediately (ransomware encryption typically follows within minutes of EDR kill); force-reboot to reload the AV kernel components; do NOT trust the EDR's own response action — it may have been disabled. 3) HUNT — look for new local admin creations, SystemBC C2 beacons (article ties Gentlemen to a 1,570-host SystemBC botnet), shadow-copy deletion (vssadmin), and lateral RDP/SMB from this host to other endpoints; check FortiGate VPN auth logs for recent logons given the FortiBleed-credential targeting.
let VendorProcs = dynamic(["MsMpEng.exe","NisSrv.exe","SenseIR.exe","SenseCncProxy.exe","MsSense.exe","CSFalconService.exe","CSFalconContainer.exe","SentinelAgent.exe","SentinelServiceHost.exe","SentinelStaticEngine.exe","cyserver.exe","cyveraservice.exe","CortexXDR.exe","SophosAgent.exe","SophosFS.exe","SophosHealth.exe","SophosClean.exe","tmlisten.exe","PccNTMon.exe","TmCCSF.exe","ekrn.exe","egui.exe","eelam.exe","bdagent.exe","vsserv.exe","epsecurityservice.exe","masvc.exe","mcshield.exe","mfemms.exe","FrameworkService.exe","avp.exe","avpui.exe","kavfs.exe","klnagent.exe"]);
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType == "ProcessTerminated" or ActionType == "ProcessCreated"
| where FileName in~ (VendorProcs)
| summarize TerminatedProcs = make_set(FileName), VendorProcCount = dcount(FileName), FirstKill = min(Timestamp), LastKill = max(Timestamp) by DeviceName, bin(Timestamp, 5m)
| where VendorProcCount >= 10
| order by FirstKill desc
let VendorProcs = dynamic(["MsMpEng.exe","NisSrv.exe","SenseIR.exe","SenseCncProxy.exe","MsSense.exe","CSFalconService.exe","CSFalconContainer.exe","SentinelAgent.exe","SentinelServiceHost.exe","SentinelStaticEngine.exe","cyserver.exe","cyveraservice.exe","CortexXDR.exe","SophosAgent.exe","SophosFS.exe","SophosHealth.exe","SophosClean.exe","tmlisten.exe","PccNTMon.exe","TmCCSF.exe","ekrn.exe","egui.exe","eelam.exe","bdagent.exe","vsserv.exe","epsecurityservice.exe","masvc.exe","mcshield.exe","mfemms.exe","FrameworkService.exe","avp.exe","avpui.exe","kavfs.exe","klnagent.exe"]);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4689
| extend ProcShort = tostring(split(ProcessName, "\\")[-1])
| where ProcShort in~ (VendorProcs)
| summarize TerminatedProcs = make_set(ProcShort), VendorProcCount = dcount(ProcShort), FirstKill = min(TimeGenerated), LastKill = max(TimeGenerated) by Computer, bin(TimeGenerated, 5m)
| where VendorProcCount >= 10
| order by FirstKill desc

Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s) Reconnaissance High
Match vulnerability scanner output to the CVE(s) named in the article.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2022-42045", "CVE-2025-26125")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2022-42045", "CVE-2025-26125")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc
APPLICATION
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Vulnerabilities
    where Vulnerabilities.signature IN ("CVE-2022-42045", "CVE-2025-26125")
    by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.signature, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.cve
| `drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities)`
| sort - severity
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Vulnerabilities
    where Vulnerabilities.signature IN ("CVE-2022-42045", "CVE-2025-26125")
    by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.signature, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.cve

| sort - severity
Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

references:

Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement Actions on Objectives High
psexec / paexec / smbexec / wmic /node — service install over SMB from remote host.
ATT&CKT1021.002 T1569.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")
   or (FileName =~ "wmic.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "/node:")

SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)

union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,

    ( ImProcessCreate

        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Gemini-MCP-tool @file exfiltration of sensitive paths (CVE-2026-0755) AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts for Gemini CLI invoked under gemini-mcp-tool with @-prefixed references to sensitive local files (id_rsa, .env, /etc/passwd, .aws/credentials, path-traversal). In vulnerable versions 1.1.2–1.1.5 untrusted prompt content reached the @file parser and could exfiltrate arbitrary files outside the working directory. Rationale: GHSA-4h5r-5jm8-jxjm explicitly cites @/etc/passwd, @~/.ssh/id_rsa and @../../secret as the canonical exfil patterns. Pairing the sensitive-path token with a node/npx/gemini-mcp-tool parent yields a narrow, high-fidelity detection rooted directly in the advisory text — no external corroboration needed.
ATT&CKT1005 T1552.004 T1083
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developers testing the patched 1.1.6+ build with legitimate @-references to files happening to contain 'env' in their name
  • Security teams verifying CVE-2026-0755 fix with intentional exfil probes (should be tagged in change-mgmt)
  • Documentation examples being copy-pasted into prompts that reference /etc/passwd
  • CTF/training environments using gemini-mcp-tool against intentionally-vulnerable hosts
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("--dry-run","--test","vuln-verify","cve-2026-0755-test"))
Response runbook
1. TRIAGE: Pull the full ProcessCommandLine and parent chain. Run `npm ls -g gemini-mcp-tool` and per-project `npm ls gemini-mcp-tool` on the host to confirm version <1.1.6. Identify the prompt source — was it stdin, an IDE plugin, a chat UI, or a file? Untrusted prompt input is the injection vector. 2. CONTAIN: Force-upgrade to gemini-mcp-tool >=1.1.6 (`npm i -g gemini-mcp-tool@latest`). Rotate any credentials referenced in the @file paths (SSH keys, .env secrets, .aws/credentials). Snapshot host. 3. HUNT: Search egress to Gemini API (generativelanguage.googleapis.com) for POST bodies matching exfil'd file sizes from the same node PID. Pivot on user across chat-tool / IDE / web logs for prompt-injection patterns in the last 30d. Inventory all hosts running vulnerable versions via SBOM / TVM.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","npx.exe") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "gemini-mcp-tool"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("@/etc/passwd","@~/.ssh/","@/root/","@/proc/self/","@../","@./../","id_rsa",".aws\\credentials",".env")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "@"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          ParentImage = InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          ChildImage = FolderPath,
          ChildCmd = ProcessCommandLine,
          SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\\node.exe","\\npx.exe") or CommandLine has "gemini-mcp-tool"
| where CommandLine has_any ("@/etc/passwd","@~/.ssh/","@/root/","@/proc/self/","@../","@./../","id_rsa",".aws\\credentials",".env")
| where CommandLine has "@"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())

Windows cmd.exe metacharacter break-out via gemini-mcp-tool (CVE-2026-0755) AIExploitation High
On Windows, vulnerable gemini-mcp-tool (1.1.2–1.1.5) failed to quote cmd.exe arguments correctly, allowing untrusted prompt content containing shell metacharacters to break out of the argument and execute attacker commands. Hunts for cmd.exe spawned by node.exe with metacharacter+LOLBin payload signatures. Rationale: Advisory explicitly says: 'On Windows, unquoted cmd.exe metacharacters could break out into OS command injection.' Pairing node.exe→cmd.exe parent-child with metachar+LOLBin combinations (|powershell, &curl, &certutil, &bitsadmin) drives FPs down vs raw metacharacter matching, since legitimate npm scripts rarely chain cmd to download-capable LOLBins.
ATT&CKT1059.003 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • npm/yarn scripts using 'cmd /c ... && powershell.exe ...' intentionally for cross-shell pipelines
  • Electron / desktop Node apps invoking cmd.exe with curl for self-update
  • CI runners on developer hosts (Jenkins agents, GitHub Actions self-hosted) chaining cmd to powershell during builds
  • Vulnerability test harnesses replaying the CVE-2026-0755 PoC against patched hosts
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("npm run","yarn run","pnpm run","electron-builder","webpack"))
Response runbook
1. TRIAGE: Inspect the cmd.exe ChildCmd for the post-metachar payload — which LOLBin? what URL/hash? Confirm gemini-mcp-tool version on host via `npm ls -g gemini-mcp-tool`. Determine whether the prompt that triggered execution came from a trusted source or untrusted input (clipboard, file, web fetch, MCP client). 2. CONTAIN: Kill cmd.exe and child PIDs. Quarantine any downloaded payload. Upgrade gemini-mcp-tool to >=1.1.6. If a remote payload landed, isolate the host. 3. HUNT: Pivot on the injected payload URL/hash across the fleet. Check for persistence created within ±10min of the spawn (Run keys via DeviceRegistryEvents, scheduled tasks via DeviceEvents ActionType=ScheduledTaskCreated). Inventory all hosts with gemini-mcp-tool 1.1.2–1.1.5 via DeviceTvmSoftwareInventory and prioritise patching.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "node.exe"
| where FileName =~ "cmd.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("|powershell","&powershell","&&powershell","|curl","&curl","|certutil","&certutil","|bitsadmin","&bitsadmin","|mshta","&mshta","|wget","&wget")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          ParentImage = InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          ChildImage = FolderPath,
          ChildCmd = ProcessCommandLine,
          SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\\node.exe"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\cmd.exe"
| where CommandLine has_any ("|powershell","&powershell","&&powershell","|curl","&curl","|certutil","&certutil","|bitsadmin","&bitsadmin","|mshta","&mshta","|wget","&wget")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine

DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-0755")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-0755")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc
