Anomalous bulk export / cross-geo admin access to TinyPulse (WebMD) SaaS tenant AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the trusted-relationship abuse pattern Shadowbyt3$ used against Nintendo's TinyPulse tenant: bulk download/export or multi-country interactive sign-ins to the TinyPulse / WebMD Health Services employee-survey platform. Targets the SaaS audit telemetry where the actual collection occurred — Nintendo's endpoints saw nothing. Rationale: Pinned to the exact SaaS the article names (TinyPulse owned by WebMD Health Services). The article confirms Nintendo's endpoints were untouched, so the only place this attack is visible to Nintendo is in TinyPulse's SaaS audit feed and the SSO sign-in path used to reach it. Cross-geo / bulk-export signals match the kill-chain phase-1B detection hint verbatim.
ATT&CKT1199 T1213 T1530
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • HR / People-Ops admin running scheduled survey exports for analytics
  • Authorized data-migration off TinyPulse (Nintendo may now be doing exactly this post-breach)
  • Sales/CS user logging into WebMD/TinyPulse customer portal from a business trip — legitimate cross-geo
  • Service account performing API-driven analytics extracts that exceed the volumetric threshold
  • MSP / consultant tenant access from a different geography during a configured engagement
Suppression filter
| where AccountUpn !in~ ("hr-survey-admin@nintendo.com","peopleops-export@nintendo.com") and IPs !has_any ("<allowlisted-vendor-CIDR>")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the user is an authorized TinyPulse admin (HR/People-Ops). Pull the matching IP geolocations, the user-agent string, and the TinyPulse audit-log line item for the export action. Compare against the user's normal sign-in baseline from SigninLogs over 90 days. 2) Contain: if the access is not pre-approved, force a password reset + revoke active sessions for the TinyPulse SSO app in Entra, and contact WebMD/TinyPulse support to revoke API tokens and pull tenant-side audit logs. 3) Hunt: pivot on the source IP across SigninLogs / CloudAppEvents for other SaaS apps (especially HR / payroll / benefits platforms — adjacent supply-chain targets), and check whether the same actor accessed any other shared third-party tenant in the last 30 days.
let TinyPulseApps = dynamic(["TinyPulse","tinypulse","WebMD","webmd","WebMD Health Services"]);
let BulkOps = dynamic(["Export","BulkDownload","MassDownload","DownloadFile","ExportToCsv","ExportData","DownloadReport"]);
let SignInAnomaly = AADSignInEventsBeta
  | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
  | where Application has_any (TinyPulseApps) or ApplicationId has_any (TinyPulseApps)
  | where ErrorCode == 0
  | summarize SignInCount = count(),
              Countries = make_set(Country, 10),
              IPs = make_set(IPAddress, 25),
              FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp)
              by AccountUpn, Application
  | where array_length(Countries) > 2 or SignInCount > 200
  | extend Signal = "cross-geo or volumetric sign-in";
let BulkExport = CloudAppEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
  | where Application has_any (TinyPulseApps)
  | where ActionType has_any (BulkOps)
     or (ActivityType has_any ("download","export","bulk") and isnotempty(ObjectName))
  | summarize EventCount = count(),
              Objects = make_set(ObjectName, 25),
              Countries = make_set(CountryCode, 10),
              IPs = make_set(IPAddress, 10),
              FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp)
              by AccountDisplayName, Application, ActionType
  | extend Signal = "bulk export against TinyPulse";
SignInAnomaly
| union BulkExport
| order by LastSeen desc
let TinyPulseApps = dynamic(["TinyPulse","tinypulse","WebMD","webmd","WebMD Health Services"]);
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where AppDisplayName has_any (TinyPulseApps) or ResourceDisplayName has_any (TinyPulseApps)
| where ResultType == 0
| extend Country = tostring(parse_json(tostring(LocationDetails)).countryOrRegion)
| summarize SignInCount = count(),
            Countries = make_set(Country, 10),
            IPs = make_set(IPAddress, 25),
            FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated)
            by UserPrincipalName, AppDisplayName
| where array_length(Countries) > 2 or SignInCount > 200
| order by LastSeen desc
(source:azure.activeDirectory OR source:okta) (@properties.appDisplayName:(*TinyPulse* OR *tinypulse* OR *WebMD* OR *webmd*) OR @target.displayName:(*TinyPulse* OR *WebMD*)) @evt.outcome:success
#event_simpleName=IdpAuthenticationLog (TargetAppName=/tinypulse|webmd/i OR ApplicationName=/tinypulse|webmd/i) Result=Success
| groupBy([UserPrincipal, TargetAppName], function=[count(), count(field=CountryCode, distinct=true, as=CountryCount), collect([CountryCode, RemoteAddressIP4])])
| CountryCount > 2 OR _count > 200
CLOUD
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Authentication.src) as src values(Authentication.src_ip) as src_ip dc(Authentication.src_ip) as ip_count dc(Authentication.src_country) as country_count from datamodel=Authentication where Authentication.app IN ("*TinyPulse*","*tinypulse*","*WebMD*","*webmd*") Authentication.action="success" by Authentication.user Authentication.app | `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)` | where country_count > 2 OR ip_count > 10 | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Authentication.src) as src values(Authentication.src_ip) as src_ip dc(Authentication.src_ip) as ip_count dc(Authentication.src_country) as country_count from datamodel=Authentication where Authentication.app IN ("*TinyPulse*","*tinypulse*","*WebMD*","*webmd*") Authentication.action="success" by Authentication.user Authentication.app | `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)` | where country_count > 2 OR ip_count > 10 | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
First-time outbound to mega.nz file-sharing infrastructure (Shadowbyt3$ leak host) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects first-seen connections from any corporate device to mega.nz / mega.io / mega.co.nz — the file-sharing service Shadowbyt3$ uses to host their data-leak samples (named explicitly in the Nintendo breach post). Catches both (a) employees clicking the leak link to verify exposure and (b) any potential attacker reuse of mega.nz for exfil/staging from corporate infrastructure. Rationale: mega.nz is the exact host the article names — Shadowbyt3$ posted the leaked Nintendo employee data sample there. The first-seen anti-join eliminates noise from established personal-use patterns and surfaces the post-breach scenario (employees clicking the leak link, or attacker reuse against another corporate target). Pivots on RemoteUrl and DNS for redundancy.
ATT&CKT1567.002 T1567
Data sourcesWeb.Web Network_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Employee personally using mega.nz for legitimate file storage on a BYOD or hybrid device
  • Security / IR team member fetching the leak sample for verification under approved IR
  • Marketing / creative team using mega.nz to receive large files from external vendors
  • Researcher or threat-intel analyst downloading public leak archives
  • Open-source project that hosts release binaries on mega.nz
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("--headless","/silent","/quiet")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the user/device making the connection and check whether it was browser-initiated (likely a curious employee clicking the leak link) or process-initiated (potential automated exfil/staging). Pull the SHA256 of InitiatingProcessFileName and check it against known browsers. 2) Contain: if the process is non-browser or unsigned, isolate the device via Defender LiveResponse pending review; if browser, send the user a phishing-awareness reminder and confirm no leak-data was downloaded to local disk. 3) Hunt: query DeviceFileEvents for files written to disk from a mega.nz origin URL on the same host (FileOriginUrl has_any mega.nz) and look for archive files (.zip / .rar / .7z) written within the same window; pivot on the source IP for any other anonymous file-sharing destinations (anonfiles, gofile.io, pixeldrain).
let MegaPatterns = dynamic(["mega.nz","mega.io","mega.co.nz","g.api.mega.co.nz","userstorage.mega.co.nz"]);
let Baseline = DeviceNetworkEvents
    | where Timestamp between (ago(90d) .. ago(7d))
    | where RemoteUrl has_any (MegaPatterns)
    | summarize by DeviceId;
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any (MegaPatterns) or RemoteUrl matches regex @"(?i)\bmega\.(?:nz|io|co\.nz)\b"
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| join kind=leftanti Baseline on DeviceId
| summarize FirstSeen = min(Timestamp),
            LastSeen = max(Timestamp),
            ConnCount = count(),
            URLs = make_set(RemoteUrl, 10),
            IPs = make_set(RemoteIP, 10),
            Processes = make_set(InitiatingProcessFileName, 5),
            CmdLines = make_set(InitiatingProcessCommandLine, 5)
            by DeviceId, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by FirstSeen desc
let MegaPatterns = dynamic(["mega.nz","mega.io","mega.co.nz","g.api.mega.co.nz"]);
let Baseline = (union isfuzzy=true
    (CommonSecurityLog | where TimeGenerated between (ago(90d) .. ago(7d)) | where RequestURL has_any (MegaPatterns) or DestinationHostName has_any (MegaPatterns) | summarize by SourceIP),
    (DnsEvents | where TimeGenerated between (ago(90d) .. ago(7d)) | where Name has_any (MegaPatterns) | summarize by ClientIP=tostring(ClientIP))
  )
  | summarize by SourceIP;
union isfuzzy=true
  (CommonSecurityLog
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where RequestURL has_any (MegaPatterns) or DestinationHostName has_any (MegaPatterns)
    | project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, SourceUserName, RequestURL, DestinationHostName, DestinationIP, SentBytes, ReceivedBytes, Source="Proxy"),
  (DnsEvents
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where Name has_any (MegaPatterns)
    | project TimeGenerated, SourceIP=tostring(ClientIP), RequestURL=Name, Source="DNS")
| join kind=leftanti Baseline on SourceIP
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), Hits=count(), URLs=make_set(RequestURL, 10), Bytes=sum(coalesce(SentBytes,0)) by SourceIP, SourceUserName
| order by FirstSeen desc
title: First-time outbound connection to mega.nz (Shadowbyt3$ leak-host infrastructure)
id: 6f2d9c1a-8e74-4b03-9a5f-b7d2e9c4a1b6
status: experimental
description: Detects connections to mega.nz / mega.io / mega.co.nz file-sharing infrastructure, used by the Shadowbyt3$ extortion-as-a-service group to host stolen-data leak samples (e.g. the Nintendo of America TinyPulse breach, June 2026).
references:
  - https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/nintendo-confirms-data-stolen-in-webmd-subsidiary-cyberattack/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/18
tags:
  - attack.exfiltration
  - attack.t1567.002
  - attack.t1567
logsource:
  category: network_connection
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_url:
    DestinationHostname|contains:
      - mega.nz
      - mega.io
      - mega.co.nz
  condition: selection_url
falsepositives:
  - Personal use of mega.nz file-sharing on a corporate device
  - Legitimate research / IR team verifying the leak sample
level: medium
(source:windows.sysmon @EventID:3 (@DestinationHostname:(*mega.nz* OR *mega.io* OR *mega.co.nz*) OR @QueryName:(*mega.nz* OR *mega.io* OR *mega.co.nz*))) OR (source:cisco.umbrella @dns.question.name:(*mega.nz* OR *mega.io* OR *mega.co.nz*))
(#event_simpleName=DnsRequest DomainName=/(^|\.)mega\.(nz|io|co\.nz)$/i) OR (#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4 ContextImageFileName=/.*/) 
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, DomainName], function=[count(), min(@timestamp, as=FirstSeen), max(@timestamp, as=LastSeen)])
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Web.user) as user values(Web.url) as url values(Web.bytes_out) as bytes_out sum(Web.bytes_out) as total_bytes from datamodel=Web where (Web.url IN ("*mega.nz*","*mega.io*","*mega.co.nz*","*g.api.mega.co.nz*") OR Web.dest IN ("mega.nz","mega.io","mega.co.nz")) by Web.src Web.dest Web.url | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | where total_bytes > 1048576 OR firstTime > relative_time(now(), "-7d")
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Web.user) as user values(Web.url) as url values(Web.bytes_out) as bytes_out sum(Web.bytes_out) as total_bytes from datamodel=Web where (Web.url IN ("*mega.nz*","*mega.io*","*mega.co.nz*","*g.api.mega.co.nz*") OR Web.dest IN ("mega.nz","mega.io","mega.co.nz")) by Web.src Web.dest Web.url | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | where total_bytes > 1048576 OR firstTime > relative_time(now(), "-7d")
Inbound email referencing Shadowbyt3$ extortion / leak negotiation AIActions on Objectives High
Alerts on inbound email mentioning the Shadowbyt3$ threat actor name, ransom amount, or known leak-site language combined with mega.nz URLs — the exact extortion-contact pattern the article describes (48-hour negotiation window, $2M demand). Catches the initial extortion approach to Nintendo and any subsequent victim outreach by the same actor. Rationale: Shadowbyt3$ is the named actor; '48 hours', '$2 million', 'extortion as a service', and 'Deleted Permanently' are direct quotes from the article's ransom note. The mega.nz URL join confirms it's the same leak-distribution pattern. Very low FP risk because the actor name is unique.
ATT&CKT1657 T1486
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • IR / threat-intel team forwarding the BleepingComputer article internally for awareness
  • Vendor security-bulletin / SOC newsletter referencing the Nintendo breach
  • Legitimate inbound contact from journalists writing follow-up coverage
  • Phishing simulation that intentionally mimics extortion language for training
Suppression filter
| where SenderFromDomain !endswith "nintendo.com" and not (SenderFromAddress has_any ("@bleepingcomputer.com","@krebsonsecurity.com","securityalerts@"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: open the message, capture headers (especially Authentication-Results and Return-Path), verify the sender domain, and check whether the body contains a contact channel (Tox ID, qTox, Session, onion address, mega.nz link). Confirm whether the message reached an executive, legal, or comms inbox — those are the actor's typical targets. 2) Contain: quarantine the message tenant-wide via M365 Threat Explorer / soft-delete; alert legal + executive protection + comms before any reply is sent; do NOT engage with the threat actor. 3) Hunt: search EmailEvents for other inbound messages from the same SenderFromDomain or with the same mega.nz URL across the past 90 days; check whether any third-party HR/engagement SaaS (BambooHR, Culture Amp, Lattice, Officevibe) shows similar bulk-export or anomalous-geo sign-in activity — Shadowbyt3$ telegraphed 'more victims' so adjacent SaaS pivots are likely.
let ExtortionKeywords = dynamic(["Shadowbyt3","shadowbyt3","ShadowByt3$","shadow byt3"]);
let RansomLanguage = dynamic(["48 hours","48-hour","$2 million","2,000,000","extortion as a service","Deleted Permanently","leak site","data leak"]);
EmailEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
| where Subject has_any (ExtortionKeywords)
    or Subject has_any (RansomLanguage)
| join kind=leftouter (
    EmailUrlInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
    | where Url has_any ("mega.nz","mega.io","mega.co.nz")
    | project NetworkMessageId, LeakUrl=Url
  ) on NetworkMessageId
| project Timestamp, NetworkMessageId, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
          RecipientEmailAddress, Subject, DeliveryAction, DeliveryLocation,
          LeakUrl, ThreatTypes
| order by Timestamp desc
let ExtortionKeywords = dynamic(["Shadowbyt3","shadowbyt3","ShadowByt3"]);
let RansomLanguage = dynamic(["48 hours","$2 million","2,000,000","extortion as a service","Deleted Permanently","data leak"]);
OfficeActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
| where Subject has_any (ExtortionKeywords) or Subject has_any (RansomLanguage)
| project TimeGenerated, UserId, ClientIP, Operation, Subject, Sender=tostring(Sender), Recipients=tostring(Recipients), MessageId=tostring(InternetMessageId)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

references:

Close Encounters of the Human Kind

Cisco Talos
2026-06-18 3 use cases 2 techniques 3 kill-chain phases detected

In the latest Threat Source, Hazel channels her inner Spielberg to explore why humans are delightfully irrational, reminding us that while security best practices are simple in theory, they’re a lot harder to pull off when you’re busy dealing with real life.

ATT&CKT1190 T1555.003

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Article-specific behavioural hunt — Close Encounters of the Human Kind
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Talos top-prevalence malware hash sweep — VID001.exe coinminer + f_000cd7.html (week of 2026-06-18) · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Talos top-prevalence malware hash sweep — VID001.exe coinminer + f_000cd7.html (week of 2026-06-18) AIInstallation High
Hunts for execution or file-write activity matching the two complete SHA256 hashes Talos identified as most prevalent in their telemetry this week: a Win.Worm.Coinminer dropper observed as VID001.exe and a malicious HTML payload observed as f_000cd7.html (W32.C0AD494457-95.SBX.TG). Pure hash-IOC sweep — the article gives no behavioural context to pivot on. Rationale: Article is a Talos weekly newsletter — bulk is commentary / headlines with no IOCs. The only article-specific detectable content is the 'Most prevalent malware files from Talos telemetry over the past week' block, which lists two complete SHA256 + MD5 pairs (the third is truncated and unusable). Hashes are concrete, high-fidelity strings directly from the article. Filename hints (VID001.exe, f_000cd7.html) added to SPL/Sigma as supplemental selectors. No web corroboration performed — these are Talos's own first-party telemetry hashes and there's no campaign context to enrich.
ATT&CKT1496 T1204.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Malware analyst workstations intentionally detonating samples (researcher sandbox VMs)
  • VirusTotal / threat-intel platform API workers caching the sample locally
  • SOC purple-team exercises replaying Talos prevalence-list IOCs to validate detection coverage
  • Endpoint backup/EDR quarantine restore operations re-materialising the file on disk
  • Pre-existing dormant infection from prior week being newly flagged as the hash is added to the watchlist
Suppression filter
| where DeviceName !has "sandbox" and DeviceName !has "analyst" and DeviceName !has "malware-lab"
| join kind=leftanti (DeviceInfo | where MachineGroup has_any ("Threat Research", "Malware Analysis", "Sandbox")) on DeviceId
Response runbook
1. Triage: pull the full process tree around the hit — parent process, command line, write origin (FileOriginUrl on DeviceFileEvents). Confirm device is production (not analyst/sandbox) via DeviceInfo.DeviceCategory and machine group. Check Talos reputation page links and pivot the SHA256 in VT for current verdict. 2. Contain: isolate the host via Defender Live Response / Falcon RTR if execution is confirmed (not just a stale file on disk). Kill the running process, quarantine the file, capture memory if coinminer behaviour suspected (high CPU, outbound to mining pools). 3. Hunt: pivot on the parent process / download URL and SHA256 of the dropper across the fleet to find sibling infections; query DeviceNetworkEvents for the host's outbound traffic in the hour around the file write for stratum+tcp:// mining-pool destinations (T1496) or unfamiliar C2 beacons; check DeviceRegistryEvents for Run-key persistence written by the same InitiatingProcessId.

Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] NGINX worker process spawning shell, scripting interpreter, or download utility
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs
NGINX worker process spawning shell, scripting interpreter, or download utility AIExploitation High
Hunts for nginx master or worker processes spawning a shell, scripting interpreter, or networked download tool — the canonical post-exploitation footprint when CVE-2026-42530 (HTTP/3 QPACK use-after-free) or CVE-2026-42055 (HTTP/2 proxy heap overflow) results in code execution inside the nginx process tree. Article-specific to F5/NGINX RCE flaws rather than generic web-shell hunting. Rationale: Article names ngx_http_v3_module (QPACK UAF) and ngx_http_proxy_v2_module / ngx_http_grpc_module (heap overflow) as the RCE vehicles inside the nginx process — so any child process spawned BY nginx other than its own workers is a high-fidelity post-exploitation signal. Cross-checked with F5 advisory K000150000 and the prior CVE-2026-42945 (NGINX Rift) exploitation pattern noted in the article. Cross-checked against: • https://my.f5.com/manage/s/article/K000150000 • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-42530 • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-42055
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.001 T1059.004 T1505.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Operator-installed nginx wrappers (e.g. systemd ExecStartPre scripts) that legitimately call sh/bash for cert rotation
  • CI/CD config push agents that invoke `nginx -s reload` via a shell helper
  • Container init scripts where nginx is PID 1 and execs sh during graceful shutdown
  • Custom lua-resty modules shelling out to curl for upstream health checks
  • Certbot/acme.sh renewals that nginx invokes as a deploy-hook
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("-s reload", "-s reopen", "-t") or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("certbot", "acme.sh", "renew", "deploy-hook"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the full nginx→child process tree, child command line, and SHA256. Confirm host runs an affected build (NGINX OSS 1.30.x/1.31.x, NGINX Plus R33-R37, Ingress Controller 3.5-5.5, App Protect 4.10-5.8, Gateway Fabric 1.3-2.6). Compare child process to host's documented nginx deploy hooks. 2) Contain: if child is not on the host's nginx-hook allowlist, isolate the host from the network, snapshot memory, and rotate any TLS keys / upstream credentials reachable from the nginx context. 3) Hunt: pivot on the source IP that opened the active HTTP/3 (UDP/443) or HTTP/2 session immediately preceding the spawn; sweep all internet-facing nginx hosts for the same parent→child tuple in the last 30 days; check `nginx -V` for `--with-http_v3_module` and audit `proxy_http_version 2` / `grpc_pass` / `ignore_invalid_headers off` / `large_client_header_buffers` in deployed configs.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("nginx.exe", "nginx")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe", "powershell.exe", "pwsh.exe", "bash", "sh", "dash", "zsh", "wget", "curl", "python", "python3", "perl", "ruby", "nc", "ncat", "wscript.exe", "cscript.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("nginx.exe", "nginx")
| where TargetProcessName has_any ("cmd.exe", "powershell.exe", "pwsh.exe", "bash", "sh", "dash", "zsh", "wget", "curl", "python", "python3", "perl", "ruby", "nc", "ncat", "wscript.exe", "cscript.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine, Hash
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Inventory of hosts running NGINX versions vulnerable to CVE-2026-42530 / CVE-2026-42055 AIReconnaissance High
Surfaces all managed devices reporting an NGINX OSS, NGINX Plus, NGINX Instance Manager, Ingress Controller, Gateway Fabric, App Protect WAF/DoS, or F5 WAF for NGINX build in the affected version ranges. Drives the patch-now worklist instead of waiting for exploitation telemetry, since the article notes F5 NGINX CVE-2026-42945 (NGINX Rift) came under active exploitation within days of disclosure. Rationale: Article enumerates the exact affected product/version ranges (NGINX OSS 1.30.0-1.30.2 / 1.31.0-1.31.1, NGINX Plus 37.0.0-37.0.1 and R33-R36, Instance Manager 2.17-2.22, Ingress Controller 3.5-5.5, Gateway Fabric 1.3-2.6, App Protect WAF 4.10-5.8, App Protect DoS 4.3-4.7, F5 WAF for NGINX 5.9-5.13.1, F5 DoS for NGINX 4.9.0). Pivoting on DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities and SoftwareName='nginx*' surfaces them directly. Cross-checked against F5 K000150000. Cross-checked against: • https://my.f5.com/manage/s/article/K000150000 • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-42530 • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-42055
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Devices showing nginx via bundled container images that have already been replaced but TVM hasn't re-scanned
  • Lab/sandbox hosts intentionally kept on vulnerable builds for security research
  • NGINX Plus subscriptions where the fix-track (R36 P6) was applied without a version bump
  • Hosts running nginx behind a WAF that already mitigates the unauth attack surface
  • Embedded nginx in vendor appliances where the customer cannot patch directly
Response runbook
1) Triage: rank hits by IsInternetFacing=true, then by whether HTTP/3 (`--with-http_v3_module`) or HTTP/2 proxy directives (`proxy_http_version 2`, `grpc_pass`, `ignore_invalid_headers off`, `large_client_header_buffers >2MB`) are present in the deployed config. 2) Contain: for internet-facing vulnerable hosts that cannot be patched within 24h, apply F5's documented mitigations — disable HTTP/3 (`listen ... quic` removed) for CVE-2026-42530 and remove `ignore_invalid_headers off` or shrink `large_client_header_buffers` below 2 MB for CVE-2026-42055. 3) Hunt: cross-reference the inventory against egress logs to confirm whether ASLR is enforced on each host (ASLR-disabled or bypassable hosts are the actually-exploitable subset); run UC1 retroactively across all surfaced hosts for the last 30 days.

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Crawl4AI /crawl endpoint POST with Chromium launcher-switch payload in body (GHSA-r253-r9jw-qg44)
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Chromium process invoked with --no-zygote AND subprocess-launcher override flag co-occurrence (Crawl4AI RCE)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Chromium subprocess override spawns non-Chromium child (Crawl4AI RCE post-exploitation)
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Crawl4AI /crawl endpoint POST with Chromium launcher-switch payload in body (GHSA-r253-r9jw-qg44) AIDelivery High
Hunts inbound HTTP POST requests targeting Crawl4AI's /crawl, /crawl/stream, /crawl/job endpoints whose body or query string carries Chromium subprocess-launcher override switches (--utility-cmd-prefix, --renderer-cmd-prefix, --gpu-launcher, --browser-subprocess-path) and/or --no-zygote. This is the literal exploit shape for the unauthenticated RCE in pip:crawl4ai <= 0.8.9 — only WAF/reverse-proxy or API-gateway logs that capture the request body will see the payload. Rationale: Pivots on the three vulnerable endpoints named verbatim in the advisory (/crawl, /crawl/stream, /crawl/job) AND the exact Chromium switch list called out in the Summary (--utility-cmd-prefix, --renderer-cmd-prefix, --gpu-launcher, --browser-subprocess-path) plus --no-zygote, which the advisory explicitly identifies as the attack enabler. Co-occurrence of the endpoint and any one of these switches is near-zero in legitimate traffic — the patched 0.9.0 hard-rejects any request body containing extra_args, so even trusted callers do not transmit them over the wire.
ATT&CKT1190 T1659 T1203
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal vuln scanners (Nuclei, Tenable, Qualys) replaying the public PoC against patched 0.9.0 hosts
  • Red team / pentest engagements probing exposed Crawl4AI Docker hosts
  • Crawl4AI Docker upgrade validation traffic from CI/CD pipelines
  • Trusted in-process SDK callers were never supposed to traverse the WAF — anything that does is anomalous
  • Security researchers fuzzing the advisory's PoC from research VPC ranges
Suppression filter
| where not (RequestClientApplication has_any ("Nuclei", "Nessus", "Qualys", "Tenable"))
Response runbook
1. TRIAGE — Pull the full request body from WAF/proxy. Confirm it is a POST to /crawl* and the JSON payload literally contains browser_config.extra_args with one of the four launcher-switch keys. Identify the responding Crawl4AI host: get the running crawl4ai package version (pip show crawl4ai or docker image tag). If <= 0.8.9, treat as confirmed exploit attempt. 2. CONTAIN — Block source IP at the WAF. If version <= 0.8.9 AND a HTTP 200 was returned, isolate the container, snapshot it for forensics, and rotate every secret, token, and mounted credential reachable from the container's runtime user. Patch to 0.9.0 immediately or set CRAWL4AI_API_TOKEN and front the API with auth. 3. HUNT — On the container host hunt DeviceProcessEvents/auditd for chromium processes with --no-zygote co-occurring with any launcher-prefix switch (see UC #2), then walk child processes for shells, curl/wget, nc, base64 piping, and outbound connections to non-Chromium-update destinations.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemotePort in (80, 8000, 8080, 11235, 443, 8443)
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("/crawl", "/crawl/stream", "/crawl/job")
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("--utility-cmd-prefix", "--renderer-cmd-prefix", "--gpu-launcher", "--browser-subprocess-path", "--no-zygote", "extra_args")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, LocalIP, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where RequestMethod =~ "POST"
| where RequestURL has_any ("/crawl", "/crawl/stream", "/crawl/job")
| where Message has_any ("--utility-cmd-prefix", "--renderer-cmd-prefix", "--gpu-launcher", "--browser-subprocess-path", "--no-zygote") or Message has "extra_args"
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, RequestMethod, RequestURL, RequestClientApplication, Message
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Chromium process invoked with --no-zygote AND subprocess-launcher override flag co-occurrence (Crawl4AI RCE) AIExploitation High
High-fidelity behavioural detection for the exploit primitive in GHSA-r253-r9jw-qg44. The vulnerability turns into RCE only when a Chromium process is launched with --no-zygote (disables the sandbox-forking zygote) simultaneously with one of the four subprocess-launcher overrides (--utility-cmd-prefix, --renderer-cmd-prefix, --gpu-launcher, --browser-subprocess-path). That tuple is pathognomonic — legitimate Chromium use cases for these flags are limited to Chromium build/test farms, not production crawler containers. Rationale: The advisory's Summary names the exact switch set verbatim: '--utility-cmd-prefix, --renderer-cmd-prefix, --gpu-launcher, --browser-subprocess-path' combined with '--no-zygote'. Co-occurrence of --no-zygote with any of those four launcher overrides on a Chromium process image is the minimal sufficient condition for the exploit to land — the advisory states '--no-zygote, causing Chromium to fork/exec an attacker-controlled command'. Outside Chromium development this tuple is essentially never benign.
ATT&CKT1203 T1059 T1611
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Chromium browser developers running headless build / regression tests with these flags
  • Internal red-team replaying the public PoC against patched 0.9.0 to validate the fix
  • Chromium fuzzing harnesses (ClusterFuzz, libFuzzer wrappers) that legitimately tweak subprocess launchers
  • Pentest training labs intentionally hosting the vulnerable image
  • Crawl4AI maintainer self-testing in a sandboxed lab container
Suppression filter
| where not (DeviceName has_any ("chromium-build", "chrome-buildbot", "cluster-fuzz")) and not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("clusterfuzz", "libfuzzer"))
Response runbook
1. TRIAGE — Pull the full ProcessCommandLine and the InitiatingProcessParent chain. Confirm the parent is Crawl4AI's Python entrypoint (uvicorn / gunicorn / python -m crawl4ai). Capture the command that follows the launcher-prefix flag — that string is the attacker's RCE payload. Pull the package version (pip show crawl4ai inside the container); if <= 0.8.9, treat as confirmed RCE. 2. CONTAIN — Kill the parent Crawl4AI service, isolate the container/host from the network, snapshot the container filesystem and memory for forensics. Rotate every secret reachable from the container runtime user: env vars, mounted config files, IAM/SP tokens, DB creds, cloud metadata-service tokens (IMDSv2). Patch the image to crawl4ai >= 0.9.0 and set CRAWL4AI_API_TOKEN. 3. HUNT — Walk DeviceProcessEvents children of the Chromium PID for shells (bash, sh, busybox, cmd.exe), staging tools (curl, wget, nc, ncat, base64, python -c), and credential-access (cat /proc/self/environ, /var/run/secrets/**, AWS meta

Chromium subprocess override spawns non-Chromium child (Crawl4AI RCE post-exploitation) AIInstallation High
Process-tree detection for the moment the Crawl4AI exploit lands: a Chromium parent invoked with --browser-subprocess-path / --renderer-cmd-prefix / --utility-cmd-prefix / --gpu-launcher fork/execs a child that is NOT another Chromium binary. The launcher-prefix switches are specifically designed to replace the child-process launch command, so any non-Chromium child of such a parent is the attacker's payload running as the container runtime user. Rationale: The advisory says the launcher-prefix flags 'replace a child-process launch command...causing Chromium to fork/exec an attacker-controlled command as the container's runtime user'. The detection encodes that directly: parent is Chromium, parent cmdline contains one of the four advisory-named switches, child is not another Chromium helper. This is the on-disk fingerprint of the RCE actually executing.
ATT&CKT1203 T1059 T1611
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Chromium browser developers' build/regression harnesses (these flags are documented Chromium dev features)
  • Headless Chromium fuzzing infrastructure (ClusterFuzz / libFuzzer wrappers)
  • Internal red-team replay of the PoC against patched 0.9.0 instances
  • Chromium release pipelines running automated subprocess tests
  • Researchers detonating the public PoC in isolated honeypot containers
Suppression filter
| where not (DeviceName has_any ("chromium-build", "chrome-buildbot", "clusterfuzz")) and not (FileName in~ ("clusterfuzz", "libfuzzer", "asan_symbolize"))
Response runbook
1. TRIAGE — Capture the child ProcessCommandLine — that is the attacker's RCE payload. Common shapes: /bin/sh -c '<curl|wget> <stager>', python -c, bash with base64, /usr/bin/id, /bin/cat /proc/self/environ. Identify the host: get container ID via DeviceName / aid and confirm it is running crawl4ai <= 0.8.9. 2. CONTAIN — Kill the Crawl4AI container, pull a forensic snapshot, isolate the node from network. Rotate ALL secrets reachable from the container runtime user (env, mounted secrets, cloud IMDS tokens, DB creds, OAuth tokens). Block the source IP at WAF. Patch image to crawl4ai >= 0.9.0 and set CRAWL4AI_API_TOKEN. 3. HUNT — From the child PID walk its descendants: shells, reverse-shell tools (nc, ncat, socat, python -c 'import socket'), staging downloads (curl/wget to non-Chromium-update destinations), credential access (cat /var/run/secrets/**, IMDS 169.254.169.254). Pivot DeviceNetworkEvents off the container for new outbound destinations in the 30 minutes after exploit time. Sea

Crawl4AI Python process writes to Linux persistence path (GHSA-2jq4-q6vv-4cp3 exploitation) AIInstallation High
Detects the actual on-disk artifact of the Crawl4AI path-traversal RCE: a python process whose command line references crawl4ai writing to a cron drop-in, profile.d, an SSH authorized_keys, or a shell rc-file. These targets are explicitly named in the advisory as the RCE escalation paths from arbitrary file write. Rationale: Article explicitly enumerates the RCE escalation paths: 'overwriting a shell rc-file, ~/.ssh/authorized_keys, a cron entry, or a Python module on the import path.' The path list, combined with python/uvicorn/gunicorn as the writing process (the runtime under which crawl4ai executes per the affected file crawl4ai/async_crawler_strategy.py), is high-fidelity because legitimate python web services do not write to these locations. The crawl4ai cmdline tag elevates severity but is not required for the alert. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-2jq4-q6vv-4cp3 • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/crawl4ai/GHSA-365w-hqf6-vxfg/ • https://dev.to/cverports/ghsa-vx9w-5cx4-9796-crawl4ai-when-web-scrapers-become-file-servers-3kh0
ATT&CKT1505 T1098.004 T1053.003 T1546.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Ansible / Chef / Puppet runs that shell out via a python wrapper to deploy cron drop-ins to /etc/cron.d/
  • cloud-init or container entrypoint scripts populating /etc/profile.d/ on first boot
  • SaltStack pip-installed states writing authorized_keys via python user.present
  • Pip-installed config-management tools deploying shell rc-files for service users
  • Developer running crawl4ai locally with a quirky configured downloads_path that happens to overlap a profile location
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any ("/usr/lib/ansible","/usr/lib/salt","/opt/puppetlabs","/var/lib/cloud/") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("ansible","salt-call","puppet","cloud-init"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full DeviceFileEvents / ImFileEvent for the host within 1h either side of the hit; read the written file's contents (is it an attacker shell key, a cron line invoking curl|bash, a tampered rc-file?); run `pip show crawl4ai` on the host to confirm vulnerable version <=0.8.9 and check whether the Docker /crawl endpoint is reachable without CRAWL4AI_API_TOKEN. 2) Contain: stop the crawl4ai service/container, revert the written file from backup, rotate any SSH keys present in authorized_keys, remove unknown cron entries, and immediately upgrade to 0.9.0 OR set CRAWL4AI_API_TOKEN as the temporary workaround. 3) Hunt: pivot on UC2 inventory to find every other host running crawl4ai <=0.8.9, replay UC3 to find any spawned shells/reverse-connects, and review web/proxy logs for inbound POSTs to /crawl from external IPs that immediately preceded the write.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName startswith "python" or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("uvicorn","gunicorn")
| where (FolderPath has_any ("/etc/cron.d/","/etc/cron.daily/","/etc/cron.hourly/","/etc/cron.weekly/","/etc/cron.monthly/","/etc/profile.d/"))
    or (FolderPath has "/.ssh/" and FileName =~ "authorized_keys")
    or (FileName in~ (".bashrc",".bash_profile",".profile",".zshrc",".bash_login") and FolderPath !startswith "/etc/skel")
| extend Crawl4AIContext = iff(InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("crawl4ai","async_crawler_strategy","docker_server:app"), "crawl4ai", "other-python")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, ActionType, FolderPath, FileName, SHA256, Crawl4AIContext
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("python","uvicorn","gunicorn")
| where (TargetFilePath has_any ("/etc/cron.d/","/etc/cron.daily/","/etc/cron.hourly/","/etc/cron.weekly/","/etc/cron.monthly/","/etc/profile.d/"))
    or (TargetFilePath has "/.ssh/" and TargetFileName =~ "authorized_keys")
    or (TargetFileName in~ (".bashrc",".bash_profile",".profile",".zshrc",".bash_login") and TargetFilePath !startswith "/etc/skel")
| extend Crawl4AIContext = iff(ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("crawl4ai","async_crawler_strategy","docker_server:app"), "crawl4ai", "other-python")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, EventType, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA256, Crawl4AIContext
| order by TimeGenerated desc

description: Detects a python/uvicorn/gunicorn process writing to a cron drop-in, profile.d, SSH authorized_keys, or a shell rc-file. Matches the RCE escalation paths called out in Crawl4AI advisory GHSA-2jq4-q6vv-4cp3 (arbitrary file write via attacker-controlled Content-Disposition / suggested_filename).
references:
    - https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-2jq4-q6vv-4cp3
author: Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/18
tags:
    - attack.persistence
    - attack.t1505
    - attack.t1098.004
    - attack.t1053.003
    - attack.t1546.004
logsource:
    product: linux
    category: file_event
detection:
    selection_proc:
        Image|contains:
            - '/python'
            - '/uvicorn'
            - '/gunicorn'
    selection_cron:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '/etc/cron.d/'
            - '/etc/cron.daily/'
            - '/etc/cron.hourly/'
            - '/etc/cron.weekly/'
            - '/etc/cron.monthly/'
            - '/etc/profile.d/'
    selection_ssh:
        TargetFilename|endswith: '/.ssh/authorized_keys'
    selection_rc:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '/.bashrc'
            - '/.bash_profile'
            - '/.profile'
            - '/.zshrc'
            - '/.bash_login'
    filter_skel:
        TargetFilename|startswith: '/etc/skel/'
    condition: selection_proc and (selection_cron or selection_ssh or selection_rc) and not filter_skel
falsepositives:
    - Ansible/Chef/Puppet runs invoking python to lay down cron drop-ins (should originate from /usr/bin/ansible-* not from a crawl4ai container)
    - Legitimate first-boot cloud-init python scripts populating /etc/profile.d/
level: high
source:linux.auditd (@process.executable.path:(*/python* OR */uvicorn OR */gunicorn) OR @process.name:(python* OR uvicorn OR gunicorn)) (@file.path:(*/etc/cron.d/* OR */etc/cron.daily/* OR */etc/cron.hourly/* OR */etc/cron.weekly/* OR */etc/cron.monthly/* OR */etc/profile.d/* OR */.ssh/authorized_keys OR */.bashrc OR */.bash_profile OR */.profile OR */.zshrc OR */.bash_login)) -@file.path:/etc/skel/*
#event_simpleName=FileWritten
| ContextImageFileName=/(python|uvicorn|gunicorn)/i
| regex("(/etc/cron\\.(d|daily|hourly|weekly|monthly)/|/etc/profile\\.d/|/\\.ssh/authorized_keys$|/\\.bashrc$|/\\.bash_profile$|/\\.profile$|/\\.zshrc$|/\\.bash_login$)", field=TargetFileName)
| NOT regex("^/etc/skel/", field=TargetFileName)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, ContextProcessId, TargetFileName], function=count())
| sort(_count, order=desc)
ENDPOINT

Vulnerable Crawl4AI package inventory (<= 0.8.9, pre-patch for GHSA-2jq4-q6vv-4cp3) AIReconnaissance High
Inventory hunt for hosts running pip:crawl4ai at or below 0.8.9, the affected range called out in the advisory. Output the device list so the SOC can prioritise patching to 0.9.0 or applying the CRAWL4AI_API_TOKEN workaround before the file-write detection (UC1) catches actual exploitation. Rationale: Advisory pins the affected range as pip:crawl4ai <= 0.8.9 with the fix in 0.9.0. Inventory hunt narrowed by package_manager=pip + name=crawl4ai is exact — no false matches against unrelated software. Joining DeviceInfo to flag internet-facing hosts surfaces the highest-priority targets first since the Docker /crawl HTTP sink is reachable unauthenticated by default. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-2jq4-q6vv-4cp3
ATT&CKT1190
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer workstations with crawl4ai installed in a venv for testing — usually low-value but still worth tracking
  • Already-patched hosts where DeviceTvmSoftwareInventory hasn't refreshed yet (DAR sync lag, typical 12-24h)
  • Forked/vendored copies of crawl4ai that pin to an old version intentionally but aren't reachable from the internet
  • CI build agents that pip-install crawl4ai per job and tear down — appear in inventory briefly
Response runbook
1) Triage: enumerate each affected device — confirm whether it's a server running the Docker image (high risk, default-unauth /crawl endpoint) vs a dev workstation using the SDK against attacker-controlled URLs (medium risk). 2) Contain: schedule emergency upgrade to >=0.9.0 for any internet-facing server; for hosts that can't immediately patch, set CRAWL4AI_API_TOKEN and confine the downloads_path to a dedicated volume mounted nosuid/nodev as an unprivileged user. 3) Hunt: for each affected host, run UC1 over the last 30 days to surface any historical file-write exploitation that pre-dated this detection going live.
DeviceTvmSoftwareInventory
| where SoftwareName =~ "crawl4ai"
| extend MajorVer = toint(extract(@"^(\d+)", 1, SoftwareVersion))
| extend MinorVer = toint(extract(@"^\d+\.(\d+)", 1, SoftwareVersion))
| extend PatchVer = toint(extract(@"^\d+\.\d+\.(\d+)", 1, SoftwareVersion))
| where MajorVer == 0 and (MinorVer < 8 or (MinorVer == 8 and PatchVer <= 9))
| join kind=leftouter (DeviceInfo | summarize arg_max(Timestamp, OSPlatform, PublicIP, IsInternetFacing) by DeviceId) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, IsInternetFacing, PublicIP
| order by IsInternetFacing desc, DeviceName asc
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where SoftwareName =~ "crawl4ai"
| extend MajorVer = toint(extract(@"^(\d+)", 1, SoftwareVersion)), MinorVer = toint(extract(@"^\d+\.(\d+)", 1, SoftwareVersion)), PatchVer = toint(extract(@"^\d+\.\d+\.(\d+)", 1, SoftwareVersion))
| where MajorVer == 0 and (MinorVer < 8 or (MinorVer == 8 and PatchVer <= 9))
| join kind=leftouter (DeviceInfo | summarize arg_max(TimeGenerated, OSPlatform, IsInternetFacing, PublicIP) by DeviceId) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, IsInternetFacing, PublicIP
| order by IsInternetFacing desc
#event_simpleName=InstalledApplication SoftwareName=/^crawl4ai$/i
| regex("^0\\.([0-7]\\.|8\\.[0-9]$|8\\.[0-9][^0-9])", field=SoftwareVersion)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion], function=count())
APPLICATION
| inputlookup software_inventory.csv where package_manager="pip" AND package_name="crawl4ai" | rex field=package_version "^(?<major>\d+)\.(?<minor>\d+)\.(?<patch>\d+)" | where major=0 AND (minor<8 OR (minor=8 AND patch<=9)) | table host package_name package_version last_seen | sort - last_seen
Python crawl4ai process spawns shell or persistence helper (post-exploitation child) AIExploitation Medium
Detects the post-exploitation pivot from the Crawl4AI arbitrary file write: the python/uvicorn worker that exposed the vulnerable HTTP / Playwright crawler spawning a shell, crontab, ssh-keygen, or curl/wget. The vulnerable runtime should not normally fork these binaries. Rationale: Advisory names crawl4ai/async_crawler_strategy.py as the vulnerable file and the unauthenticated Docker /crawl endpoint (which runs the FastAPI app via uvicorn) as the reachable sink. A normal Crawl4AI worker does not exec shells, crontab, ssh-keygen, or curl — those are the obvious next steps after writing an attacker-controlled file (chmod the dropped payload, trigger the cron, fetch a second stage). Constrained to the parent-cmdline crawl4ai marker so it does not fire on generic python child-process noise. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-2jq4-q6vv-4cp3 • https://dev.to/cverports/ghsa-5882-5rx9-xgxp-crawl4ai-rce-hook-line-and-sinker-into-your-docker-container-3l1l
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1190 T1053.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Crawl4AI legitimately invoking Playwright's bundled headless-chromium launcher which forks shell-like helpers on some distros
  • Container entrypoint scripts using sh -c to wrap the python crawl4ai server startup — would appear as parent=python child=sh once at boot
  • Developer using crawl4ai notebook / REPL that shells out via os.system or subprocess.run for debugging
  • Crawl4AI extension hooks (custom on_page hooks) that legitimately call curl/wget — should be reviewed and allow-listed by parent cmdline of the specific hook script
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/playwright/driver","playwright install","chromium --type=")) and not (FileName == "sh" and ProcessCommandLine has "-c" and ProcessCommandLine has "uvicorn")
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the full process tree (DeviceProcessEvents | extend ProcessGroup = … or `pstree` on host); read the child command line for indicators of fetch-and-exec (curl|bash, wget -O -, chmod +x then ./payload); correlate to UC1 hits on the same host within 5min either side. 2) Contain: kill the crawl4ai worker, isolate the host from network, snapshot memory + disk, rotate any credentials accessible from that container (env vars, mounted secrets, IMDS). 3) Hunt: pivot on outbound NetworkConnectIP4 from the python process during the same window to identify attacker C2; review web logs for the upstream POST /crawl that triggered exploitation and the attacker URL that returned the malicious Content-Disposition.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName startswith "python" or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("uvicorn","gunicorn")
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("crawl4ai","async_crawler_strategy","docker_server:app")
| where FileName in~ ("bash","sh","dash","zsh","ksh","crontab","ssh-keygen","curl","wget","nc","ncat","socat","chmod")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessId, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("python","uvicorn","gunicorn")
| where ParentProcessCommandLine has_any ("crawl4ai","async_crawler_strategy","docker_server:app")
| where TargetProcessName has_any ("/bash","/sh","/dash","/zsh","/ksh","/crontab","/ssh-keygen","/curl","/wget","/nc","/ncat","/socat","/chmod")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

HTTP request with spoofed 'auth-user: service-brother' header (@acastellon/auth GHSA-gfj5-979r-92pw) AIExploitation High
Detects HTTP requests carrying the literal 'auth-user: service-brother' header — the exact marker that short-circuits validateToken() in @acastellon/auth <2.3.0 before legacy/JWT/OIDC validation runs. Any external/unauthenticated request matching this signature is exploitation of the bypass. Rationale: Targets the article's exact bypass marker — the literal 'auth-user: service-brother' header value that the GHSA names as the validateToken() short-circuit trigger. Detection must run at WAF/proxy/app layer because Defender XDR endpoint tables do not capture custom HTTP request headers (noted in defender_kql comment). The Sentinel union covers four realistic landing places: CommonSecurityLog (third-party WAFs), AzureDiagnostics (App Gateway / Front Door WAF / App Service), ImWebSession (ASIM normalised), and W3CIISLog (IIS in front of Node). No external sources cross-checked — niche npm GHSA with no CVE, no campaign attribution, and no second-source coverage expected.
ATT&CKT1190 T1078 T1556
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate internal service-to-service calls from the real service-brother microservice originating from RFC1918 / known service CIDR
  • Application security testing tools (Burp, OWASP ZAP, Nuclei) replaying the public PoC against pre-prod environments
  • Internal red-team or purple-team exercises verifying the v2.3.0 patch landed
  • Vendor pentest engagements including this advisory in their test plan
  • SOC itself replaying the marker through WAF to validate a new block rule
Suppression filter
| where ExternalSrc == "yes"
Response runbook
1) Triage: Pull source IP, destination hostname, full URL. Run `npm ls @acastellon/auth` on the destination host — if version >= 2.3.0 the bypass is patched and this is likely scanner noise. Check the ExternalSrc enrichment column: internal source + known service-brother CIDR = closeable. 2) Contain: External source + destination version < 2.3.0 = confirmed exploitation. Block source IP at WAF/edge, rotate any session tokens or JWTs minted by the application in the suspect time window, force re-auth on the affected app, and capture full request bodies for IR. 3) Hunt: Pivot on source IP for 24h of activity across all applications. Search for follow-up requests carrying 'is-admin: true' or other 'is-*' privilege-claim headers from the same IP (see UC3). Review downstream services that trust the auth-user header for anomalous service-brother activity (DB writes, admin actions, token mints).
// @acastellon/auth ships as a Node.js dependency — HTTP request headers are NOT in Defender XDR endpoint tables. This query surfaces internet-facing Node.js listeners on hosts likely to be running the vulnerable middleware; the actual header inspection must run on WAF/proxy logs (see sentinel_kql / datadog_query).
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","nodejs.exe","pm2.exe")
| where LocalPort in (80,443,3000,4000,5000,8080,8443)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| where ActionType == "InboundConnectionAccepted" or ActionType == "ConnectionAccepted"
| summarize InboundConns=count(), DistinctRemoteIPs=dcount(RemoteIP), arg_max(Timestamp, RemoteIP, RemotePort) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, LocalPort
| where InboundConns > 0
| extend Advisory="GHSA-gfj5-979r-92pw — verify @acastellon/auth dependency on this host"
| order by InboundConns desc
let bypassMarker = "service-brother";
(union isfuzzy=true
    (CommonSecurityLog
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
        | where (Message has bypassMarker and Message has "auth-user")
             or DeviceCustomString1 has bypassMarker
             or DeviceCustomString2 has bypassMarker
             or DeviceCustomString3 has bypassMarker
             or DeviceCustomString4 has bypassMarker
             or RequestContext has bypassMarker
             or RequestCookies has bypassMarker
        | project TimeGenerated, SourceTable="CommonSecurityLog", SrcIP=SourceIP, DstHost=DestinationHostName, URL=RequestURL, Method=RequestMethod, UA=RequestClientApplication, Vendor=DeviceVendor, Raw=Message),
    (AzureDiagnostics
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
        | where Category in ("ApplicationGatewayFirewallLog","FrontdoorWebApplicationFirewallLog","AppServiceHTTPLogs","FrontDoorAccessLog","FrontdoorAccessLog")
        | where tostring(Properties) has bypassMarker
        | project TimeGenerated, SourceTable=Category, SrcIP=tostring(Properties.clientIP), DstHost=tostring(Properties.host), URL=tostring(Properties.requestUri), Method=tostring(Properties.httpMethod), UA=tostring(Properties.userAgent), Vendor="Azure", Raw=tostring(Properties)),
    (ImWebSession
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
        | where HttpRequestHeaderAuthorization has bypassMarker
             or HttpRequestHeaderCookie has bypassMarker
        | project TimeGenerated, SourceTable="ImWebSession", SrcIP=SrcIpAddr, DstHost=DstHostname, URL=Url, Method=HttpMethod, UA=HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, Vendor=EventVendor, Raw=HttpRequestHeaderAuthorization),
    (W3CIISLog
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
        | where csUriQuery has bypassMarker or csUserAgent has bypassMarker

Vulnerable @acastellon/auth (<2.3.0) package on disk + internet-facing Node.js listener AIWeaponization High
Hunts hosts where the @acastellon/auth dependency tree is present on disk (node_modules/@acastellon/auth/package.json or auth.js) and joins against internet-facing Node.js listener telemetry to prioritise the most exposed targets. This is the actual attack surface for GHSA-gfj5-979r-92pw and feeds the patching workstream. Rationale: Targets the article's specifically-named affected package '@acastellon/auth v2.2.0' by hunting the npm install footprint on disk (node_modules/@acastellon/auth/package.json and auth.js). The Defender query cross-joins with internet-facing Node.js listener telemetry to prioritise the most-exposed hosts for emergency patching. Path matching uses contains+all rather than literal escaped paths because npm's @-scoped package directory naming is consistent enough (and avoids fragile JSON/regex backslash escaping). No external corroboration searched — GHSA is the only authoritative source for this niche package.
ATT&CKT1190 T1195.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Dev / sandbox / lab hosts intentionally kept at v2.2.0 for regression testing of the v2.3.0 fix
  • Backup or archived application snapshots being restored on a non-production host
  • Security researcher / red-team / purple-team host reproducing the advisory PoC
  • Container image build caches that retain old node_modules layers despite the running container shipping v2.3.0
  • Internal package mirror or artifact registry that holds all historical versions for auditing
Suppression filter
| where DvcHostname !contains "-dev" and DvcHostname !contains "-sandbox" and DvcHostname !contains "-lab" and DvcHostname !contains "-qa"
Response runbook
1) Triage: Read package.json on the affected device — `Get-Content '<path>\node_modules\@acastellon\auth\package.json' | ConvertFrom-Json | Select version` (or `jq .version` on Linux). If version >= 2.3.0 close as patched. 2) Contain: version < 2.3.0 AND InternetFacing == 'yes' → page the app owner, fast-track the bump to 2.3.0+, AND in the meantime front the app with a WAF rule blocking inbound requests carrying 'auth-user: service-brother' (mitigates exposure while patching). 3) Hunt: For every vulnerable+internet-facing host, run UC1 across the prior 90 days against the destination FQDN. Any hits = treat as candidate compromise, escalate to IR, and review downstream services that trust the auth-user/is-* headers for anomalous service-brother activity.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FolderPath contains "node_modules" and FolderPath contains "acastellon" and FolderPath contains "auth"
| where FileName in~ ("package.json","auth.js")
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), arg_max(Timestamp, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName) by DeviceName, FileName
| join kind=leftouter (
    DeviceNetworkEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","nodejs.exe")
    | where LocalPort in (80,443,3000,4000,5000,8080,8443)
    | where RemoteIPType == "Public"
    | summarize NodeInboundConns=count() by DeviceName
) on DeviceName
| extend InternetFacing = iif(isnotempty(NodeInboundConns) and NodeInboundConns > 0, "yes", "unknown"), Advisory="GHSA-gfj5-979r-92pw — @acastellon/auth < 2.3.0"
| project DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, FirstSeen, LastSeen, NodeInboundConns, InternetFacing, Advisory
| order by InternetFacing desc, LastSeen desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFilePath contains "node_modules" and TargetFilePath contains "acastellon" and TargetFilePath contains "auth"
| where TargetFileName in~ ("package.json","auth.js")
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), arg_max(TimeGenerated, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessName) by DvcHostname, TargetFileName
| extend Advisory="GHSA-gfj5-979r-92pw — @acastellon/auth < 2.3.0 (check package.json version field)"
| order by LastSeen desc

Spoofable privilege-claim headers (is-admin / is-*) downstream of @acastellon/auth bypass AIExploitation Medium
Detects HTTP requests carrying 'is-admin: true' or other 'is-*' privilege-asserting headers. The article's v2.3.0 fix explicitly adds sanitisation for incoming 'is-*' headers because the vulnerable middleware passed them through to downstream services that trusted them, enabling privilege escalation once validateToken() was bypassed. Co-occurrence with 'service-brother' makes this the highest-confidence post-bypass primitive. Rationale: Targets the article's explicit fix note: 'Always sanitize incoming auth-user and is-* headers' — meaning the v2.3.0 patch identifies 'is-*' headers as a privilege-escalation primitive when paired with downstream services that trust them. The 'is-admin: true' header appears verbatim in the article's example request. PairedWithBypass enrichment promotes the highest-confidence hit (is-* co-occurring with service-brother in the same request). The Sentinel query filters out internal traffic without bypass co-occurrence to keep FP rate down. No external corroboration searched — niche GHSA with no CVE / campaign mapping.
ATT&CKT1078.004 T1556 T1548
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal frontend → backend service-mesh traffic where some apps legitimately propagate 'is-' prefixed feature-flag headers (e.g. 'is-feature-x: true')
  • Health-check / synthetic monitoring tooling that exercises admin endpoints with explicit privilege flags
  • QA test harnesses that set 'is-admin: true' against staging to bypass paywall / role checks
  • Pentest / bug-bounty researcher demonstrating the advisory PoC
  • WAF rule auditing where the SOC itself replays the marker headers to validate the new block rule
Suppression filter
| where PairedWithBypass == "yes" or ExternalSrc == "yes"
Response runbook
1) Triage: Check if source IP is internal (service-mesh) or external. Pull the destination URL — admin / internal API paths are highest-risk. If the same source IP also fired UC1 (auth-user: service-brother) within ±5 minutes, OR PairedWithBypass == 'yes' on this event, escalate immediately as confirmed exploitation chain. 2) Contain: External source + admin-path destination → block source IP at WAF, invalidate any sessions / API tokens / role grants minted on the destination service since the first hit, force re-auth. Notify the application owner that downstream services trusting 'is-*' headers must either be hardened or fronted by a header-stripping proxy. 3) Hunt: Across the prior 7 days, search for 'is-*: true' headers from the same source IP against any application. Review downstream service logs on the destination host (DB writes, role assignments, token mints, admin UI actions) for activity consistent with an elevated principal that the actual auth-user wouldn't have authorised.
let privHeaders = dynamic(["is-admin","is-superuser","is-staff","is-root","is-internal","is-service"]);
let truthy = dynamic(["true","1","yes"]);
(union isfuzzy=true
    (CommonSecurityLog
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
        | where Message has_any (privHeaders) and Message has_any (truthy)
        | extend PairedWithBypass=iif(Message has "service-brother","yes","no")
        | project TimeGenerated, SourceTable="CommonSecurityLog", SrcIP=SourceIP, DstHost=DestinationHostName, URL=RequestURL, Method=RequestMethod, PairedWithBypass, Raw=Message),
    (AzureDiagnostics
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
        | where Category in ("ApplicationGatewayFirewallLog","FrontdoorWebApplicationFirewallLog","AppServiceHTTPLogs","FrontdoorAccessLog")
        | extend PropsStr=tostring(Properties)
        | where PropsStr has_any (privHeaders)
        | extend PairedWithBypass=iif(PropsStr has "service-brother","yes","no")
        | project TimeGenerated, SourceTable=Category, SrcIP=tostring(Properties.clientIP), DstHost=tostring(Properties.host), URL=tostring(Properties.requestUri), Method=tostring(Properties.httpMethod), PairedWithBypass, Raw=PropsStr)
)
| extend ExternalSrc=iif(SrcIP startswith "10." or SrcIP startswith "172.16." or SrcIP startswith "172.17." or SrcIP startswith "172.18." or SrcIP startswith "172.19." or SrcIP startswith "172.20." or SrcIP startswith "172.21." or SrcIP startswith "172.22." or SrcIP startswith "172.23." or SrcIP startswith "172.24." or SrcIP startswith "172.25." or SrcIP startswith "172.26." or SrcIP startswith "172.27." or SrcIP startswith "172.28." or SrcIP startswith "172.29." or SrcIP startswith "172.30." or SrcIP startswith "172.31." or SrcIP startswith "192.168.","no","yes"), Advisory="GHSA-gfj5-979r-92pw — privilege-claim header on the wire"
| where PairedWithBypass == "yes" or ExternalSrc == "yes"
| order by PairedWithBypass desc, TimeGenerated desc
